Paper from the plantation
Once a banana plant has produced its fruit, the farmer cuts it down, because each stem fruits only once. In most of Uganda, these thick stems are simply left to rot in the fields. Grace Namutebi saw them differently.
'I was looking at a pile of old stems on my uncle's farm and I noticed how strong the fibres were,' she says. 'I wondered whether they could replace the wood that is normally used for paper.'
It took Grace almost a year of experiments in her kitchen to find the right method. The stems are first cut into strips and boiled for several hours to soften them. The fibres are then beaten into a pulp, spread thinly on screens and left to dry in the sun. The finished sheets are slightly rough and pale yellow in colour.
Grace's company now employs twenty-five people, most of them women from nearby villages. Farmers who sell their used stems to the company earn a small extra income from something they once threw away.
At first, Grace sold notebooks and greeting cards to tourists. However, her biggest customers today are hotels, which buy the paper for menus and packaging. Grace says the most difficult part of the business is not making the paper but persuading people that it is just as good as ordinary paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why do farmers cut down a banana plant after it has produced fruit?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Where did Grace first get the idea for her paper?
parts.working: Accept 'looking at old stems on her uncle's farm'. Do not accept 'in her kitchen'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is done to the strips of stem to soften them?
parts.answer: they are boiled for several hours

parts.label: d
parts.text: What colour is the finished paper?

parts.label: e
parts.text: Who are Grace's biggest customers today?
parts.working: Do not accept 'tourists' (earlier customers).

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Grace, what is the most difficult part of the business?
parts.answer: persuading people that the paper is as good as ordinary paper
parts.working: Do not accept 'making the paper'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a cycling school for adults in Lahore, and then answer the questions.

Never too old to ride
Rukhsana Bibi was fifty-two when she sat on a bicycle for the first time. 'My brothers all had bikes when we were children, but girls in our street were not allowed,' she says. 'I always felt I had missed something.'
Last spring she joined a cycling school in a quiet park in Lahore that teaches adults – most of them women – how to ride. The school was set up by Ayesha Malik, an engineer who cycles to work every day. She started it after colleagues kept asking how she had learned.
Lessons take place early on Sunday mornings, before the park becomes crowded. Beginners start on bicycles with the pedals removed, pushing themselves along with their feet until they can balance. Only then are the pedals put back on. Most learners can ride on their own after four or five lessons, although a few need more time.
The bicycles are borrowed from a local repair shop, whose owner lends them free of charge. Learners pay a small fee, which is used to buy helmets.
Rukhsana now rides to the market twice a week instead of taking a rickshaw. She says she has saved money, but the biggest change is that she feels more independent. Her next goal is to teach her granddaughter to ride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why did Rukhsana not ride a bicycle as a child?
parts.answer: girls in her street were not allowed (to ride)

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is Ayesha Malik's job?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why are lessons held early on Sunday mornings?

parts.label: d
parts.text: What do beginners do before the pedals are put back on?
parts.answer: push themselves along with their feet (until they can balance)
parts.working: Accept 'learn to balance'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the learners' fee used for?
parts.working: Do not accept 'bicycles' (lent free).

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Rukhsana, what is the biggest change in her life since learning to ride?
parts.working: Do not accept 'saving money'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a student who measures a glacier in Hunza, and then answer the questions.

Watching the ice
Twice a year, nineteen-year-old Zainab Karim climbs for six hours to reach the edge of a glacier above her village in Hunza. She carries a measuring tape, a notebook and a small camera, and she photographs the same rocks from exactly the same spot every time.
Zainab began the project at fifteen for a school science competition. Her teacher suggested placing painted stones in a line in front of the glacier and measuring the distance from each stone to the ice. Over four years, the ice has moved back by an average of eleven metres a year.
Glaciers like this one provide water for farming in the valley, especially for the apricot and potato fields. But melting ice also creates dangers. Sometimes water collects in lakes behind loose walls of rock and ice. If these walls break, a flood can rush down the valley with almost no warning.
Zainab now shares her measurements with a university in Islamabad, where scientists compare them with satellite images. 'Satellites can show large changes,' she says, 'but someone still needs to stand here and check the details.'
She is now studying geography and plans to return to Hunza after graduating. She hopes to train other young people in the valley to monitor the glaciers near their own villages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long does it take Zainab to reach the glacier?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why did Zainab start the project?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Whose idea was it to use painted stones?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which crops in the valley depend on water from the glacier?
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: e
parts.text: What can happen if the walls holding back a glacial lake break?
parts.answer: a flood rushes down the valley (with almost no warning)

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why are Zainab's measurements useful to the scientists, even though they have satellite images?
parts.answer: someone needs to check the details on the ground / satellites show only large changes

practice.stem:
Read the article about a school robotics club in Malaysia, and then answer the questions.

The robot that tests the river
When students at a secondary school in Penang, Malaysia, noticed that fish were disappearing from the river behind their school, they decided to find out why. The school's robotics club spent a term building a small floating robot, about the size of a laptop, which they named 'Kingfisher'.
Kingfisher is powered by a solar panel on its top and is steered by remote control from the riverbank. Underneath, it carries sensors that measure the temperature of the water and how much oxygen it contains. Every ten seconds, it sends these readings to a laptop on the bank.
The students quickly discovered that oxygen levels dropped sharply downstream of a pipe from a nearby factory. They presented their results to the local council, which has now asked the factory to treat its waste water before releasing it.
Building the robot was not easy. The first version tipped over in strong currents, so the team added two empty plastic bottles on each side to make it more stable. The total cost of the robot was less than the price of a single scientific sensor bought from a laboratory supplier.
The club's teacher, Mr Lim, says the project has changed how students think about science. 'They used to see it as something in a textbook,' he says. 'Now they see it as a way of solving real problems.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: What made the students want to investigate the river?
parts.answer: fish were disappearing from the river

parts.label: b
parts.text: How is the robot powered?
parts.working: Do not accept 'remote control'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one thing that the sensors measure.
parts.answer: the temperature of the water OR the amount of oxygen in the water
parts.working: Either one.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Where did oxygen levels drop sharply?
parts.answer: downstream of a pipe from a (nearby) factory

parts.label: e
parts.text: What did the team do to make the robot more stable?
parts.answer: added (two) empty plastic bottles on each side

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Mr Lim, how did students see science before the project?

practice.stem:
Read the article about a truck art workshop in Rawalpindi, and then answer the questions.

Colours on the highway
In a dusty yard near the Grand Trunk Road in Rawalpindi, Muhammad Anwar is painting a peacock on the side of a lorry. Around him, apprentices are fixing hundreds of small metal chains along the front bumper, which will jingle as the vehicle moves.
Anwar learned truck art from his father and has been doing it for thirty-five years. Decorating one lorry completely can take up to three weeks and costs the owner as much as the vehicle earns in two months. 'Drivers spend more time in their trucks than in their homes,' he says. 'They want them to be beautiful.'
Each design tells something about the owner. Pictures of mountains and rivers often remind drivers of their home villages, while lines of poetry painted on the back express their hopes or feelings. Anwar says the most requested image is still the eye, which drivers believe protects them on long journeys.
In recent years, truck art has become fashionable far beyond the highway. Anwar's workshop now receives orders to decorate kettles, furniture and even mobile phone covers, many of them for customers abroad. These small items now earn the workshop more money than the lorries do.
However, Anwar worries about the future. Fewer young people want to spend years learning the skill, and cheaper printed stickers are replacing hand painting on some vehicles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What will the metal chains on the bumper do?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who taught Anwar truck art?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How long can it take to decorate one lorry?

parts.label: d
parts.text: What do pictures of mountains and rivers often remind drivers of?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the most requested image?
parts.working: Do not accept 'peacock'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What now earns the workshop more money than lorries?
parts.answer: small (decorated) items such as kettles, furniture and phone covers
parts.working: Accept any one example or 'small items'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a seed bank run by farmers in Nepal, and then answer the questions.

Saving the seeds of the past
In a small stone building in a village in western Nepal, hundreds of glass jars line the shelves. Each one contains seeds: rice, millet, beans, barley and buckwheat, many of them varieties that most farmers stopped growing decades ago.
The community seed bank was set up by a group of twelve farmers led by Kamala Thapa. 'When I was a girl, my mother grew seven kinds of rice,' she says. 'By the time I had my own fields, the shops were selling only two.'
Modern varieties often produce bigger harvests, but they usually need chemical fertiliser and plenty of water. Some of the older varieties are better suited to the region's steep fields. One red rice, for example, grows well in cold water from mountain streams, and a local bean survives long periods without rain.
Farmers can borrow a jar of seeds for free. After the harvest, they must return twice the amount they borrowed, so the bank's collection keeps growing. The seeds are kept dry with ash from cooking fires, a method the farmers' grandparents used.
Last year, when an unusually dry summer destroyed many fields of modern rice, farmers who had planted older varieties from the seed bank still harvested a crop. Since then, demand for the jars has tripled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many farmers set up the seed bank?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many kinds of rice did Kamala's mother grow?
parts.working: Do not accept 'two'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do modern varieties usually need?
parts.answer: chemical fertiliser and plenty of water
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: What must farmers return after the harvest?
parts.answer: twice the amount (of seed) they borrowed

parts.label: e
parts.text: How are the seeds kept dry?

parts.label: f
parts.text: What happened to the demand for seeds after last year's dry summer?

practice.stem:
Read the article about the lost-property office at a large railway station, and then answer the questions.

Lost and found
Behind a plain door at one of Europe's busiest railway stations is a room that few travellers ever see. Its shelves hold umbrellas by the hundred, piles of coats and scarves, a wheelchair, two violins and, at the moment, a stuffed crocodile almost two metres long.
The lost-property office receives around 400 items every day. Staff record each one on a computer, noting where it was found and adding a short description. Items are kept for three months; after that, most are given to charity, although anything containing personal information, such as laptops, is securely destroyed.
Office manager Elena Rossi has worked there for eleven years. Surprisingly, she says, umbrellas are not the most common item. 'Everyone expects umbrellas,' she laughs, 'but we receive far more phone chargers. People plug them in on the train and simply forget them.' Umbrellas come second, and in winter, gloves move into third place.
Only about a third of all items are ever collected. Elena believes many people do not realise the office exists, while others assume that something left on a train will never be handed in. Items most likely to be reclaimed are wallets and passports; chargers are almost never collected, probably because they are cheap to replace.
The strangest phone call Elena ever received was from a man asking whether anyone had found his false teeth. Someone had.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many items does the office receive each day?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What happens to laptops that are not collected?
parts.working: Do not accept 'given to charity'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which item does the office receive most often?
parts.working: Do not accept 'umbrellas' (second).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which item becomes the third most common in winter?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What proportion of items are collected by their owners?

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why, according to the article, are chargers almost never collected?
parts.working: Do not accept 'people forget them on the train' (explains why they are lost, not why they are not collected).

practice.stem:
Read the article about sleep and teenagers, and then answer the questions.

Why teenagers can't get up
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and then cannot get out of bed in the morning. Many assume this is simply laziness. In fact, scientists say there is a biological explanation.
Everyone has an internal 'body clock' that tells us when to feel sleepy. It is controlled partly by a hormone called melatonin, which the brain releases as it gets dark. In adults and young children, melatonin levels usually rise at around nine or ten in the evening. During the teenage years, however, this happens up to two hours later. A fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at ten may simply lie awake.
Teenagers also need more sleep than adults – between eight and ten hours a night – because their bodies and brains are still developing. When school starts early, many get far less than this. Research shows that tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember information, and they are more likely to feel anxious.
Some schools have experimented with later start times. At one school, moving the start of lessons from 8.00 to 8.50 led to fewer students arriving late and better attendance, although exam results improved only slightly.
Scientists say the most helpful thing teenagers can do themselves is to avoid screens in the hour before bed, because the blue light from phones and tablets delays the release of melatonin even further.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What do many parents believe is the reason teenagers find it hard to get up?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What causes the brain to release melatonin?
parts.working: Accept 'darkness'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How much later than adults do teenagers' melatonin levels rise?
parts.working: Must include 'up to' or equivalent; accept 'as much as two hours'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why do teenagers need more sleep than adults?
parts.answer: their bodies and brains are still developing

parts.label: e
parts.text: What did NOT improve much when one school started lessons later?
parts.working: Do not accept 'attendance' or 'lateness' (these did improve).

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why should teenagers avoid screens before bed?
parts.answer: blue light delays the release of melatonin (even further)

practice.stem:
Read the article about a marine archaeologist, and then answer the questions.

Treasure under the waves
Most people imagine underwater archaeology as a search for gold coins. For Dr Mariam Haddad, the real treasure is usually much less glamorous: broken pots, ship's nails and the bones of animals that sailors ate on long voyages.
Mariam grew up in a fishing town on the coast of Lebanon. As a teenager she wanted to be a doctor, but a summer job helping divers record an old harbour wall changed her mind. She went on to study history and then trained as a professional diver, a process that took longer than her university degree.
Her team is currently studying a trading ship that sank about 1,600 years ago in water forty metres deep. At this depth, divers can work for only about twenty minutes at a time before they must return slowly to the surface. Because of this, every dive is planned carefully, and much of the recording is done with underwater cameras rather than by hand.
The ship's cargo included hundreds of clay jars called amphorae. By studying their shape, the team can tell where they were made, and tiny traces left inside show that most once contained olive oil rather than wine, as the team had first expected.
Mariam says the greatest threat to ancient wrecks today is not the sea but people. Divers who take objects as souvenirs destroy information that can never be recovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What did Mariam want to become when she was a teenager?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What experience changed Mariam's mind about her career?
parts.answer: a summer job helping divers record an old harbour wall

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which took Mariam longer: her university degree or her diving training?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why is every dive at the wreck planned carefully?
parts.answer: divers can work for only about twenty minutes at a time (at that depth)

parts.label: e
parts.text: How can the team tell where the jars were made?
parts.working: Do not accept 'traces left inside' (shows contents).

parts.label: f
parts.text: What did the team discover that surprised them?
parts.answer: most jars contained olive oil (not wine)
parts.working: Must convey olive oil. 'Wine' alone = 0.

practice.stem:
Read the article about mangrove planting on the coast of Sindh, and then answer the questions.

Forests that grow in the sea
Along the coast of the Indus Delta, where the river meets the Arabian Sea, grow forests unlike any others in Pakistan. Mangrove trees stand in salty water on tall, tangled roots, and at high tide only their green tops are visible.
These forests once covered a much larger area. During the twentieth century, dams and canals upstream reduced the amount of fresh water reaching the delta, and many trees were cut down for firewood and to feed camels. Since the 1990s, however, large replanting projects have helped the forests to recover.
Fisherman Ghulam Rasool has planted thousands of young trees himself. He explains that mangroves are important for his work, because many kinds of shrimp and fish spend the first part of their lives sheltering among the roots. 'No mangroves, no fish,' he says simply.
Mangroves also protect the coast. Their roots trap mud and slow down waves, which reduces damage when storms arrive. In addition, scientists have found that mangrove soil stores large amounts of carbon, which helps to limit climate change.
Planting is done in summer, when the soil is soft. Volunteers push seeds or young plants into the mud by hand. Ghulam says the hardest part is not the planting but stopping animals from eating the young shoots during their first year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When are only the tops of the mangrove trees visible?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What reduced the amount of fresh water reaching the delta?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from firewood, why were trees cut down?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why are mangroves important for Ghulam's work as a fisherman?
parts.answer: shrimp and fish shelter among the roots when young
parts.working: Accept 'young fish/shrimp live among the roots'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: How do mangrove roots reduce storm damage?
parts.answer: they trap mud and slow down waves
parts.working: Accept 'slow down waves' alone.

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Ghulam, what is the most difficult part of the work?
parts.answer: stopping animals eating the young shoots (in the first year)
parts.working: Do not accept 'planting'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a professional tea taster in Sri Lanka, and then answer the questions.

A life spent tasting tea
Every morning at nine, Nimal Perera sits down at a long white table on which eighty small cups have been arranged in a line. By lunchtime he will have tasted every one of them. Nimal is a professional tea taster in Colombo, and his judgement helps to decide the price of thousands of kilograms of tea each week.
Tasting is a noisy business. Nimal takes a spoonful of tea and sucks it into his mouth loudly so that it sprays across his tongue, then spits it into a large metal pot. 'Swallowing eighty cups a day would be impossible,' he explains.
Before tasting, he examines the dry leaves and smells the wet leaves left after brewing. Colour matters too: a bright, coppery colour usually means that the tea was processed well. The water is always boiled fresh, because water that has been boiled twice makes tea taste flat.
It took Nimal six years of training before he was allowed to give prices on his own. He avoids spicy food and never wears aftershave, which would interfere with his sense of smell, the most important tool in his job.
Tea from high mountain estates usually sells for the highest prices, as the cool climate makes the leaves grow slowly and develop a stronger flavour. However, Nimal says the weather in the weeks before picking can change the taste more than the height of the estate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many cups of tea does Nimal taste each morning?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does Nimal do with the tea after tasting it?
parts.answer: spits it into a (large metal) pot

parts.label: c
parts.text: What does a bright, coppery colour usually show?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why is the water always boiled fresh?
parts.answer: water boiled twice makes tea taste flat

parts.label: e
parts.text: What does Nimal consider the most important tool in his job?
parts.working: Do not accept 'taste' / 'tongue'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Nimal, what can affect the taste of tea more than the height of the estate?
parts.answer: the weather in the weeks before picking

practice.stem:
Read the article about a camel-milk dairy in the Thar Desert, and then answer the questions.

Ice cream from the desert
For centuries, herders in the Thar Desert have relied on camels for transport and milk. Until recently, however, the milk was used only by their own families, because it spoils quickly in the heat and there was no way to get it to city markets before it went sour.
That changed when Dr Kavita Kumari, a vet who grew up near Mithi, persuaded a charity to buy a small milk-cooling tank powered by solar panels. Herders now bring their milk to a collection point every morning, where it is tested for quality and chilled to 4 °C within two hours of milking.
Camel milk is saltier than cow's milk and contains less fat. It also has more vitamin C, which is valuable in a region where fresh fruit is scarce. Some people who cannot digest cow's milk find camel milk easier to drink, although Dr Kumari is careful not to claim that it cures any illness.
The dairy's best-selling product, surprisingly, is not milk but ice cream. It is flavoured with cardamom and sold in Karachi cafés, where customers pay almost four times the price of the raw milk used to make it.
The extra income has changed life for many herding families. Several now keep their children in school instead of sending them to look after the animals. The biggest remaining problem is the road: during the monsoon, the track to the main highway sometimes floods, and deliveries are delayed for days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why was camel milk not sold in city markets in the past?
parts.answer: it spoils quickly in the heat / went sour before reaching markets

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is Dr Kumari's profession?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How is the milk-cooling tank powered?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which vitamin is found in greater amounts in camel milk?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the dairy's best-selling product?
parts.working: Do not accept 'milk'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What is the biggest remaining problem for the dairy?
parts.answer: the road / the track floods in the monsoon (and deliveries are delayed)

practice.stem:
Read the article about a girls' cricket academy in Multan, and then answer the questions.

Bowling towards a dream
When the Multan Girls' Cricket Academy opened four years ago, only eleven girls came to the first practice – just enough for one team. Today it trains more than ninety players aged between ten and eighteen.
The academy was founded by Farah Qureshi, a former fast bowler who played for her province. 'When I was young, I practised with my brothers in the street, but I had no coach and no proper equipment,' she says. 'I wanted girls today to have a better start.'
Training takes place four afternoons a week on a ground lent by a local college. Players work on fitness, batting and bowling, and they also attend talks on healthy eating. The academy provides bats, pads and helmets, which are paid for by a sports shop in the city and by small donations from parents.
Persuading families was the hardest part at first. Some parents worried about their daughters' safety travelling to practice, so the academy arranged a minibus that collects players from three points in the city. Others were concerned about exams, so the girls now have a supervised homework session for an hour before training starts.
Two former players have already been selected for national youth squads. Farah says she is just as proud of the girls who have become more confident at school and in their communities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many girls came to the first practice?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things the players do at the academy apart from batting and bowling.
parts.answer: 1. work on fitness 2. attend talks on healthy eating
parts.working: 1 mark each. (Supervised homework also acceptable as a third option.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Who pays for the equipment? Give TWO answers.
parts.answer: 1. a sports shop in the city 2. (small donations from) parents
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'the college' (lends the ground).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO worries that parents had, and say how the academy dealt with each one.
parts.answer: Safety travelling to practice → minibus collecting players from three points; exams / schoolwork → supervised homework session for an hour before training
parts.working: 1 mark for each worry, 1 mark for each matching solution.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a rooftop school garden in Singapore, and then answer the questions.

A farm on the fourth floor
Space is precious in Singapore, so when a primary school in the east of the city wanted a garden, it had only one place to go: up. The flat roof of the school's four-storey building is now home to more than fifty large planting boxes.
Pupils grow pak choi, spinach, tomatoes, chillies, lemongrass and several herbs. Each class is responsible for its own box and must water it, remove weeds and record how fast the plants are growing in a notebook. Older pupils also test the soil and decide when it needs compost.
Most of the vegetables are used in the school canteen, where cooks prepare them for lunch at least twice a week. Anything left over is sold to parents at a small stall on Friday afternoons, and the money is used to buy new seeds.
Teachers say the garden has helped pupils in several ways. Children who once refused to eat green vegetables now try the ones they have grown. Mathematics lessons use real measurements from the plants, and pupils who struggle in the classroom often shine in the garden.
There have been challenges. On hot afternoons, the roof can become extremely warm, so some plants are protected by shade nets. Strong winds during storms once blew several boxes over, and they are now fixed to the floor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many floors does the school building have?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give THREE things each class must do for its planting box.
parts.answer: 1. water it 2. remove weeds 3. record how fast the plants grow (in a notebook)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not credit testing the soil or deciding about compost (done by older pupils only).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO ways the garden has helped pupils, according to teachers.
parts.answer: Any two: children try green vegetables they have grown; maths lessons use real measurements; pupils who struggle in class shine in the garden
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO problems the garden has had.
parts.answer: 1. the roof becomes extremely warm / too hot (on hot afternoons) 2. strong winds blew boxes over
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept solutions only if linked to the problem.

practice.stem:
Read the article about electric rickshaws in Bangladesh and Pakistan, and then answer the questions.

The quiet tuk-tuk
For many years, the noisy, smoky auto-rickshaw has been a familiar sight in South Asian cities. Now a quieter version is spreading. Electric rickshaws, powered by batteries instead of petrol or diesel engines, are becoming common in cities such as Dhaka and are being tested in Karachi and Lahore.
Drivers say the biggest advantage is cost. Charging a battery overnight costs much less than filling a tank with fuel, and electric motors have fewer moving parts, so repairs are cheaper too. Passengers like the fact that the ride is smoother and that they can hold a conversation without shouting.
Electric rickshaws also help the environment. Because they produce no exhaust fumes on the street, they improve air quality in crowded areas, and they reduce noise pollution.
However, there are problems. The batteries are heavy and expensive to replace, and most last only two or three years. Many drivers charge them at home using unsafe wiring, which can cause fires. In some cities, the extra demand for electricity at night has put pressure on the power supply.
Some companies are now building solar charging stations where drivers can exchange an empty battery for a full one in less than five minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What are the new rickshaws powered by?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why electric rickshaws are cheaper for drivers.
parts.answer: 1. charging costs less than fuel 2. fewer moving parts so repairs are cheaper
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO things passengers like about electric rickshaws.
parts.answer: 1. the ride is smoother 2. they can talk without shouting / it is quieter
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE problems with electric rickshaws.
parts.answer: Any three: batteries heavy; batteries expensive to replace; batteries last only two or three years; charging at home with unsafe wiring can cause fires; extra demand for electricity puts pressure on power supply
parts.working: 1 mark each. 'Heavy and expensive' counts as two points only if both stated clearly.

practice.stem:
Read the article about an app that reduces food waste, and then answer the questions.

An app against waste
Every evening, bakeries, cafés and supermarkets throw away food that is still perfectly good to eat, simply because it will not be fresh enough to sell the next day. A group of university students in Islamabad decided to do something about it.
Their mobile phone app, called 'Bachat', lists shops that have surplus food at the end of the day. Customers can reserve a 'surprise bag' for about a third of the normal price and collect it during a time slot, usually in the last hour before the shop closes. They do not know exactly what will be inside, which many users say is part of the fun.
Shop owners like the app because they earn some money from food that would otherwise be wasted, and they attract new customers who may come back to buy at full price. Some also donate bags to a local orphanage through the app.
Since its launch eighteen months ago, the app has been downloaded more than 60,000 times, and over 200 businesses have joined. The founders estimate that it has saved around 90 tonnes of food from being thrown away.
The team now hopes to expand to Lahore and Peshawar, and to add home-cooked meals from small family kitchens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When do customers usually collect their bags?
parts.answer: in the last hour before the shop closes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO details about the 'surprise bags'.
parts.answer: Any two: cost about a third of the normal price; reserved through the app; customers do not know what is inside
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why shop owners like the app.
parts.answer: 1. they earn money from food that would be wasted 2. they attract new customers (who may return)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO plans the team has for the future.
parts.answer: 1. expand to Lahore and Peshawar 2. add home-cooked meals from family kitchens
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about repair cafés, and then answer the questions.

Don't throw it away – fix it!
On the first Saturday of every month, a community hall in Utrecht in the Netherlands fills with broken things: toasters that will not toast, jeans with torn pockets, bicycles with flat tyres and lamps that refuse to light. Their owners have come to a repair café, where volunteers help them fix their belongings for free.
The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to thousands of towns around the world, including several in Pakistan and India. Volunteers are usually retired engineers, tailors, carpenters and electricians who enjoy sharing their skills.
Visitors do not simply hand over their item and wait. Instead, they sit beside the volunteer and help with the repair, so that they can do it themselves next time. While they wait for a free table, they can have tea and biscuits and chat with neighbours.
Organisers say about two-thirds of items are successfully repaired. The most common reason for failure is that spare parts are no longer available, or that the item has been glued together in the factory so that it cannot be opened without breaking it.
Supporters of repair cafés say they reduce the amount of rubbish sent to landfill, save people money and bring communities together. Some campaigners also hope they will put pressure on manufacturers to design products that last longer and are easier to repair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO kinds of volunteers who usually work at repair cafés.
parts.answer: Any two: retired engineers; tailors; carpenters; electricians
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things visitors do while waiting for a table.
parts.answer: 1. have tea and biscuits 2. chat with neighbours
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why do visitors help with the repair?
parts.answer: so that they can do it themselves next time

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why some items cannot be repaired.
parts.answer: 1. spare parts are no longer available 2. the item has been glued together in the factory / cannot be opened without breaking
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Give THREE benefits of repair cafés, according to supporters.
parts.answer: 1. reduce rubbish sent to landfill 2. save people money 3. bring communities together
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not credit 'pressure on manufacturers' (a hope of some campaigners, not a benefit stated by supporters).

practice.stem:
Read the article about a high-altitude porter in Gilgit-Baltistan, and then answer the questions.

Carrying the mountain
Each summer, thousands of climbers and trekkers travel to the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan, hoping to see K2 and the other giants of the Karakoram. Few of them would get far without people like Ali Hussain.
Ali, aged thirty-four, has worked as a porter for sixteen years. On a typical trek to K2 base camp, he carries up to twenty-five kilograms of food, tents and fuel on his back for about eight days each way. The route crosses rivers, steep rocky paths and the Baltoro Glacier, where deep cracks in the ice can be hidden under snow.
Porters face many dangers. The altitude can cause headaches, sickness and breathlessness, and sudden storms can bring freezing winds. In the past, porters were often given poor equipment, and some suffered frostbite. Today, rules require trekking companies to provide boots, warm jackets and sunglasses, and to pay insurance.
The work is well paid compared with farming, and Ali has used his earnings to send his three children to school in Skardu. However, the season lasts only from June to September, so in winter he repairs houses and looks after his family's animals.
Ali's ambition is to become a licensed mountain guide. He has started learning English from trekkers in the evenings and has taken a first-aid course run by a climbing club.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How much does Ali carry on a typical trek?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things Ali carries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO effects that altitude can have on porters.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO things that trekking companies must now provide.
parts.answer: Any two: boots; warm jackets; sunglasses; insurance
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Give TWO things Ali is doing to help him become a guide.
parts.answer: 1. learning English (from trekkers) 2. taking a first-aid course
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about coral reef restoration in the Maldives, and then answer the questions.

Gardeners of the reef
Beneath the turquoise water around the Maldives lie some of the world's most beautiful coral reefs. But in recent years, rising sea temperatures have caused large areas of coral to turn white and die, a process known as 'bleaching'.
Marine biologist Aminath Shareef leads a project that is trying to help reefs recover. Her team collects small pieces of healthy coral that have broken off naturally during storms. They tie these to metal frames shaped like tables, which are placed on the sea floor about eight metres below the surface. Over the next two years, the pieces grow and eventually join together to form new reef.
The project depends on local people. Fishermen report where storms have broken coral, and hotel guests can pay to 'adopt' a frame, which pays for materials. Students from island schools help to clean the frames, removing seaweed that would otherwise block the sunlight the coral needs.
Aminath is careful to explain that restoration alone cannot save the reefs. 'We can repair small areas,' she says, 'but unless the world reduces the gases that are warming the oceans, bleaching will keep happening.'
Even so, the frames have already brought results. Divers have counted more fish around the restored sites, and some of the new coral has survived a recent heatwave that bleached nearby natural reef.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What has caused coral to turn white and die?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO details about the frames the team uses.
parts.answer: Any two: made of metal; shaped like tables; placed on the sea floor; about eight metres below the surface
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE ways in which local people help the project.
parts.answer: 1. fishermen report where coral has broken 2. hotel guests pay to adopt a frame 3. students clean the frames / remove seaweed
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO results that show the project is working.
parts.answer: 1. divers have counted more fish around the restored sites 2. some new coral survived a heatwave (that bleached nearby reef)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about life at a research station in Antarctica, and then answer the questions.

Winter at the bottom of the world
When the last supply plane leaves the research station in late February, the twenty-two people who stay behind know they will not see anyone else for eight months. Antarctic winter is arriving, and for weeks the sun will not rise at all.
Station doctor Priya Nair is spending her first winter on the ice. As well as treating injuries, she must be ready to act as a dentist and even to perform simple operations, as no aircraft can land in the darkness and extreme cold.
The scientists at the station study the atmosphere, the ice sheet and the stars. Some collect air samples to measure pollution; others drill deep into the ice, where tiny bubbles of ancient air reveal what the climate was like thousands of years ago.
Keeping spirits up is just as important as the science. The team eats dinner together every evening, takes turns cooking and celebrates every birthday. On Saturday nights there is a film or a quiz. Priya says the hardest thing is the lack of fresh fruit and vegetables, although a small greenhouse produces lettuce and herbs under special lights.
Despite the challenges, she has no regrets. 'When the southern lights fill the sky in green and purple,' she says, 'you forget the cold completely.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long will the team not see anyone else?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO jobs Priya must be ready to do, apart from treating injuries.
parts.answer: 1. act as a dentist 2. perform simple operations
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE things the scientists study.
parts.answer: 1. the atmosphere 2. the ice sheet 3. the stars
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'pollution' for atmosphere, 'ancient climate' for ice.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the team keeps spirits up.
parts.answer: Any two: eating dinner together; taking turns cooking; celebrating birthdays; film or quiz on Saturday nights
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about the revival of calligraphy among young people, and then answer the questions.

The return of the reed pen
In an age of keyboards and touchscreens, it might seem surprising that classes in Arabic and Urdu calligraphy are fully booked in cities such as Lahore, Karachi and Peshawar. Yet teachers report that the number of young students has risen sharply over the past five years.
Calligrapher Imran Siddiqui has taught for over twenty years in a studio near the old walled city of Lahore. He believes social media is partly responsible: short videos of artists forming beautiful letters with a single stroke have attracted millions of viewers. 'People see the videos and think it looks easy,' he smiles. 'Then they discover that a single letter can take weeks to master.'
Students begin with a pen cut from a dried reed, called a qalam, and ink made from soot and gum. Imran insists on these traditional materials for the first six months because, he says, they teach patience and control in a way that a modern felt pen cannot.
Many students say calligraphy helps them relax after long hours of study. Others enjoy feeling connected to their culture and history. A few have turned their hobby into income by designing wedding invitations, shop signs and logos.
Not all traditionalists welcome these changes. Some older calligraphers complain that young artists mix styles without understanding the rules behind them. Imran disagrees. 'An art that never changes,' he says, 'is an art that is dying.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which part of Lahore is Imran's studio?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO details about the materials students use at the start.
parts.answer: Any two: a pen cut from a dried reed (qalam); ink made from soot; ink made from gum
parts.working: 1 mark each, maximum 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why does Imran insist on traditional materials?
parts.working: Accept either 'patience' or 'control'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE reasons why young people enjoy calligraphy, according to the article.
parts.answer: 1. it helps them relax after studying 2. they feel connected to their culture and history 3. some earn income from it (wedding invitations, signs, logos)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not credit 'it looks easy in videos' (why people start, not why they enjoy it).

parts.label: e
parts.text: What do some older calligraphers complain about?
parts.answer: young artists mix styles without understanding the rules

practice.stem:
Read the article about protecting farms from elephants in Sri Lanka, and then answer the questions.

Fences that bite back
For farmers in parts of Sri Lanka, a single night can destroy a whole season's work. Wild elephants, searching for food, walk out of the forest and into rice fields and vegetable gardens, eating and trampling crops. Each year, conflicts between people and elephants lead to deaths on both sides.
Traditional methods of scaring elephants away, such as lighting fires, beating drums or setting off firecrackers, often work only for a short time, as elephants soon realise that the noise is harmless. Electric fences are more effective but expensive to build and maintain, and some elephants have learned to push trees onto them to break the wire.
One cheaper solution uses an animal elephants dislike: bees. Farmers hang beehives on a wire between posts around their fields. When an elephant touches the wire, the hives swing and the angry bees fly out. Elephants have sensitive skin around their eyes and inside their trunks, and they avoid being stung.
The fences bring extra benefits. Farmers can sell the honey, which provides income, and the bees pollinate nearby crops and fruit trees, increasing harvests.
The method is not perfect. In very dry years, bee colonies sometimes leave the hives, and the fences need regular checking. But in trial villages, the number of elephant visits has fallen by more than half, and farmers say they sleep better at night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which elephants damage farms.
parts.answer: 1. they eat crops 2. they trample crops
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO traditional methods of scaring elephants.
parts.answer: Any two: lighting fires; beating drums; setting off firecrackers
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO disadvantages of electric fences.
parts.answer: Any two: expensive to build; expensive to maintain; elephants push trees onto them to break the wire
parts.working: 1 mark each. 'Expensive to build and maintain' = 1 mark unless clearly split.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO extra benefits of beehive fences.
parts.answer: 1. farmers can sell the honey / extra income 2. bees pollinate crops and fruit trees / increase harvests
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about first-aid training for young people in Pakistan, and then answer the questions.

Ten minutes that save lives
When a man collapsed at a crowded bus stop in Rawalpindi last winter, the first person to reach him was a seventeen-year-old student, Hamza Iqbal. While others filmed on their phones, Hamza checked whether the man was breathing, asked a bystander to call an ambulance on 1122, and began pressing hard and fast on the centre of his chest. By the time paramedics arrived, the man's heart was beating again.
Hamza had learned these skills only a month earlier in a free two-hour course run by volunteers at his college. The organisers, a group of young doctors, believe that every secondary-school student should be trained. 'An ambulance in a busy city may take ten minutes to arrive,' says Dr Saima Rehman. 'What happens in those ten minutes can decide whether someone survives.'
The course covers what to do if someone is choking, bleeding heavily, burned or has stopped breathing. Students practise on plastic dummies and work in pairs to practise placing an unconscious person on their side.
The doctors say the biggest obstacle is not difficulty but fear. Many people worry that they might make things worse or be blamed if the person does not recover. The trainers stress that doing something is almost always better than doing nothing.
Since the scheme began, more than 12,000 students in eight cities have been trained, and the organisers now hope to add first aid to the school timetable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give THREE things Hamza did to help the man.
parts.answer: 1. checked whether he was breathing 2. asked a bystander to call an ambulance (1122) 3. pressed hard and fast on the centre of his chest
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who runs the first-aid courses?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE situations that the course covers, apart from someone who has stopped breathing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why people are afraid to give first aid.
parts.answer: 1. they worry they might make things worse 2. they worry they might be blamed (if the person does not recover)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about an indoor vertical farm in Dubai, and then answer the questions.

Farming without fields
In a warehouse on the edge of Dubai, where summer temperatures outside reach 45 °C, rows of lettuce, rocket and basil grow in trays stacked twelve levels high. No sunlight reaches them, and there is no soil. This is a vertical farm, and it produces about three tonnes of leafy vegetables every day.
Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from red and blue LED lamps, which give the warehouse a pink glow. Red and blue are the colours plants use most for growth. Their roots hang in water containing exactly the nutrients they need. Sensors monitor temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide twenty-four hours a day, and a computer adjusts them automatically.
Supporters point out several advantages. The farm uses about 95 % less water than growing the same crops in fields, which matters in one of the driest countries on earth. No pesticides are needed, because insects cannot get in. And because the farm is close to the city, vegetables reach supermarkets within hours, rather than being flown in from abroad.
Critics, however, note that the lamps and air-conditioning use huge amounts of electricity, and unless this comes from renewable sources such as solar power, the environmental benefits are reduced. Vertical farms are also expensive to build, and so far they can grow only certain crops profitably. Wheat, rice and potatoes, for example, need too much space and light.
The company plans to cover the warehouse roof with solar panels next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why are red and blue lamps used?
parts.answer: red and blue are the colours plants use most for growth
parts.working: Do not accept 'to give a pink glow'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give THREE things the sensors monitor.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE advantages of the vertical farm, according to supporters.
parts.answer: 1. uses about 95 % less water 2. no pesticides needed (insects cannot get in) 3. vegetables reach supermarkets within hours / not flown from abroad
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO criticisms of vertical farms.
parts.answer: Any two: lamps and air-conditioning use huge amounts of electricity; expensive to build; only certain crops can be grown profitably
parts.working: 1 mark each. Examples (wheat, rice, potatoes) alone do not score unless linked to limited crops.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about rooftop gardens in Karachi, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Green roofs over a busy city

A
When Sadia Memon moved into a fourth-floor flat in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, the only outdoor space was a flat concrete roof that the building shared. In summer it became so hot that nobody went up there. Sadia asked her neighbours if she could put a few pots of mint and chillies in one corner. Most of them laughed, but nobody said no.

B
Within a year, the corner had become a small garden of tomatoes, coriander and a lemon tree in a large plastic drum. Sadia waters everything early in the morning with water left over from washing vegetables. 'Plants are not fussy about where their water comes from,' she says. She also puts a layer of dry leaves on the soil so that it does not dry out in the afternoon sun.

C
The biggest surprise was the effect on the flats below. Neighbours on the top floor noticed that their rooms felt cooler, and one family switched off their air conditioner for two hours a day. Engineers say that soil and leaves absorb heat that would otherwise pass straight through the concrete into the building.

D
Now eleven of the sixteen families in the building help with the garden, and children come up after school to pick tomatoes. Sadia runs a free workshop on the first Sunday of every month for anyone in the area who wants to start their own roof garden. Her advice is simple: 'Start with one pot. Plants teach you the rest.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section describes how Sadia saves water?
parts.working: B: 'water left over from washing vegetables'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section mentions a reaction from neighbours that was not very encouraging?
parts.working: A: 'Most of them laughed'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section explains why the garden lowered the temperature indoors?
parts.working: C: soil and leaves absorb heat that would pass through the concrete.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section says Sadia shares her knowledge with other people?
parts.working: D: free monthly workshop. Not B, which describes her methods but not teaching others.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section describes what the roof was like before the garden?
parts.working: A: flat concrete roof, so hot nobody went up.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section mentions a family using less electricity?
parts.working: C: switched off their air conditioner for two hours a day.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section gives a method of stopping the soil from losing moisture?
parts.working: B: a layer of dry leaves so the soil does not dry out.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about adults learning to swim, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Never too late to swim

A
Forty-two-year-old Farhan Ali grew up in a desert town where the nearest river was two hours away. 'There was nowhere to learn, so I never did,' he explains. When his own children started swimming lessons in Islamabad, he sat by the pool every Saturday, feeling embarrassed that he could not join them in the water.

B
Farhan's fear was not unusual. Swimming teachers say that adults often find it harder than children because they remember frightening moments, such as slipping under the water at a beach. Adults also tend to hold their breath and tense their muscles, which actually makes the body sink.

C
The adult class Farhan joined began with no swimming at all. For the first two lessons, the six learners simply stood in shallow water, blew bubbles and practised floating while holding the side. 'Our teacher told us that the water would hold us up if we let it,' Farhan says. By the fifth week he could swim a whole width.

D
Six months later, Farhan swam his first length alongside his daughter. He now goes to the pool twice a week before work and says it has helped his back pain more than any medicine. He has also persuaded two colleagues to sign up for the next beginners' course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section explains why Farhan did not learn to swim as a child?
parts.working: A: nowhere to learn; nearest river two hours away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section describes a health benefit Farhan has noticed?
parts.working: D: helped his back pain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section mentions a habit that makes swimming more difficult for adults?
parts.working: B: holding their breath and tensing muscles makes the body sink.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section describes the first activities in Farhan's class?
parts.working: C: standing in shallow water, blowing bubbles, floating.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section says Farhan encouraged other people to learn?
parts.working: D: persuaded two colleagues to sign up.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section describes how Farhan felt while watching his children?
parts.working: A: embarrassed.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section says how many people were learning in Farhan's class?
parts.working: C: the six learners.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about a school astronomy club in northern Pakistan, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Stargazing in the mountains

A
The astronomy club at a secondary school near Gilgit started with one second-hand telescope, bought by a physics teacher with money from a school cake sale. On the first evening, only four students came. Now more than thirty meet on the school's playing field on clear nights.

B
Members say the mountains are one of the best places in the country to look at the sky. There are very few street lights, and the air is dry and clean, especially in winter. 'In Lahore I could see maybe twenty stars,' says Hina, who moved to Gilgit two years ago. 'Here I can see the Milky Way with my own eyes.'

C
Watching the sky is not always comfortable. In January the temperature at night can fall well below zero, so students bring thick blankets and flasks of hot tea. They have also learned to use red torches, because white light makes it harder for their eyes to adjust to the dark.

D
Last year the club photographed the Moon through the telescope using a mobile phone, and the pictures were shown at a national science festival. The students now hope to raise money for a larger telescope so that they can see the rings of Saturn more clearly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section says the club's work was seen by people across the country?
parts.working: D: pictures shown at a national science festival.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section explains how the club got its first equipment?
parts.working: A: teacher bought it with cake-sale money.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section compares the night sky in two different places?
parts.working: B: Hina compares Lahore and Gilgit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section mentions a piece of equipment that protects the students' night vision?
parts.working: C: red torches.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section describes how the club has grown?
parts.working: A: four students at first, now more than thirty.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section gives the club's plan for the future?
parts.working: D: raise money for a larger telescope.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section mentions a difficulty caused by the weather?
parts.working: C: temperature well below zero in January.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about a school recycling project, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

From bottles to benches

A
Students at a girls' school in Faisalabad noticed that the bins outside their canteen were full of plastic water bottles every afternoon. Their science teacher challenged them to find a use for the bottles instead of sending them to the city rubbish dump.

B
After reading about similar projects online, the students decided to make 'eco-bricks': empty bottles packed tightly with clean plastic wrappers until they are as hard as wood. Each brick took about twenty minutes to fill. Families helped by saving wrappers at home and sending them to school in bags.

C
It took four months to make 600 bricks. A local builder offered to help for free, and showed the students how to join the bricks together with a mixture of clay and straw. The finished result was two long benches in the shade of the school's neem tree.

D
The benches are now the most popular place to sit at break time. The project has also changed habits: many students now bring metal water bottles from home, and the canteen has started selling drinks in glasses that are washed and reused.

parts.text: Which section describes how the project changed what students drink from?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section explains what an eco-brick is?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section mentions a professional who gave help without payment?
parts.working: C: a local builder helped for free. Not B: families helped but are not professionals.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section says where the idea for the project first came from?
parts.working: A: the science teacher's challenge after students noticed full bins.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section gives the total number of bricks made?
parts.working: C: 600 bricks.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section describes a change made by the canteen?
parts.working: D: drinks sold in reusable glasses.

parts.label: g

parts.working: B: about twenty minutes each.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about volunteers who protect sea turtles near Karachi, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Night shift on the beach

A
Every year, from about August to December, female green turtles come out of the Arabian Sea at night to lay their eggs on the sandy beaches west of Karachi. Each turtle digs a hole with her back flippers, lays around a hundred eggs, covers them with sand and returns to the sea before sunrise.

B
Nineteen-year-old Ayesha has volunteered with a turtle protection group for three seasons. Her job is to walk the beach between midnight and four in the morning with a dim torch and a notebook. When she finds a nest, she records the time and the exact place so that it can be watched.

C
The eggs face many dangers. Stray dogs dig them up, and bright lights from beach huts can confuse baby turtles when they hatch, so they crawl towards the land instead of the sea. Volunteers sometimes move eggs to a fenced area of the beach where they are safe.

D
For Ayesha, the best moment is watching the babies hatch about two months later. 'They are smaller than my hand, and they run straight for the waves,' she says. 'Only a few will survive to become adults, but every one we help gives the species a better chance.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section describes how a turtle protects her eggs after laying them?
parts.working: A: covers them with sand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section mentions why artificial light is a problem?
parts.working: C: lights confuse hatchlings so they crawl towards land.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section describes the information Ayesha writes down?
parts.working: B: records the time and exact place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section gives the size of a newly hatched turtle?
parts.working: D: smaller than my hand.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section mentions an animal that is a threat to the eggs?
parts.working: C: stray dogs.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section says how long Ayesha has been a volunteer?
parts.working: B: three seasons.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section explains why Ayesha thinks the work matters?
parts.working: D: every turtle helped gives the species a better chance.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about teenagers and sleep, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Why teenagers can't get up

A
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and are impossible to wake in the morning. Many assume this is simply laziness or too much time on phones. Scientists who study sleep, however, say the truth is more complicated, and that the teenage brain really does work on a different timetable.

B
During adolescence, the body begins to release melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, about two hours later in the evening than it did in childhood. A fourteen-year-old who tries to sleep at nine o'clock may simply lie awake. Yet teenagers still need roughly eight to ten hours of sleep a night, so an early start leaves many of them short of rest.

C
The effects of this lost sleep are not small. Tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember new information, and they are more likely to feel irritable or low. Some studies have also linked a lack of sleep to more accidents among young drivers and cyclists.

D
A few schools have experimented with starting lessons later, and several reported better attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class. Not everyone is convinced: later finishing times can clash with sports practice and part-time jobs. Experts agree, though, that teenagers themselves can help by keeping screens out of the bedroom and getting morning daylight.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section describes effects of poor sleep on mood?
parts.working: C: irritable or low.

parts.label: h

parts.working: D: better attendance, fewer students falling asleep.

Breakfast on wheels

A
At six o'clock every morning, a bright yellow van parks outside a busy office block in Gulberg, and a queue begins to form. The van belongs to twenty-four-year-old Usman Tariq, who sells fresh parathas filled with egg, spinach or spiced potato. On a good day he sells over three hundred before ten o'clock.

B
Usman did not plan to become a cook. He studied accounting and spent a year working in a bank, but he hated sitting at a desk all day. His grandmother, who had run a small dhaba in Sahiwal for thirty years, had taught him to cook as a boy, and he often thought about her kitchen while he was checking spreadsheets.

C
Starting the business was harder than he expected. He spent most of his savings on the van, and in the first month the gas cooker broke twice. Some days it rained heavily and hardly anyone came. 'My friends told me to go back to the bank,' he admits. 'I nearly did.'

D
What kept him going was his regular customers, many of whom now send him photos on social media of their breakfasts. Usman uses the accounting skills from his old job to control costs carefully, and he hopes to buy a second van next year and employ two cooks from his neighbourhood.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about scientists studying snow leopards, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Watching the ghost of the mountains

A
Snow leopards are among the hardest big cats in the world to study. They live on steep, rocky slopes high in the mountains of Central and South Asia, they are mostly active at dawn and dusk, and their grey, spotted coats blend perfectly into the rocks. Many local herders have lived in snow leopard country all their lives without ever seeing one.

B
To learn about them, researchers in northern Pakistan use camera traps: small cameras fixed to rocks that take a photograph whenever an animal walks past. Because every snow leopard has a unique pattern of spots, scientists can identify individual cats from the pictures and estimate how many live in an area.

C
The work depends on local people. Herders often know the paths that wild animals use, and they guide researchers to the best places for cameras. In return, some conservation groups help villages to build stronger animal pens, so that leopards cannot kill sheep and goats at night. This has reduced the number of leopards killed by angry farmers.

D
The photographs have produced some surprises, including images of a mother with three cubs in a valley where no snow leopards had been recorded for years. Researchers warn, though, that warmer temperatures could push the cats' prey higher up the mountains, leaving less space for both.

A sitar lesson across the ocean

A
Every Tuesday evening in Toronto, sixteen-year-old Zara Qureshi sets up her laptop on the living-room floor and tunes her sitar. Thousands of kilometres away, her teacher, Ustad Rashid, is just finishing his breakfast in Lahore. The time difference means that one of them is always a little tired, but neither has missed a lesson in two years.

B
Online lessons have obvious limits. When the internet connection is slow, the sound reaches Zara a second late, which makes playing together impossible. Her teacher cannot reach over and move her fingers into the correct position, so he has to describe exactly what he wants. 'At first I found that frustrating,' Zara admits, 'but now I listen far more carefully.'

C
There are advantages, too. Each lesson is recorded, so Zara can watch difficult passages again during the week. Ustad Rashid also teaches students in Dubai, Manchester and Karachi, and once a term they all join one video call to perform for each other. 'It feels like a little international family,' he says.

D
Zara's parents first suggested the sitar because they wanted her to stay connected to the music her grandparents loved. She was not keen at first, preferring the guitar. Now she plans to perform at her school's cultural evening next spring, and she hopes to visit Lahore to meet her teacher in person for the first time.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about planting small forests in cities, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Tiny forests, big difference

A
On a strip of wasteland beside a motorway in Lahore, where rubbish used to pile up, there is now a dense thicket of trees taller than a person. It was planted less than three years ago using a method developed by a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki, in which dozens of native species are planted very close together.

B
Because the young trees are so crowded, they compete for light and grow upwards quickly. Supporters say these 'tiny forests' can become established in a few years, rather than the decades a normal woodland needs. After the first two or three years of watering and weeding, they are expected to look after themselves.

C
City planners are interested because trees cool the air around them. On summer afternoons, paved streets and buildings in large cities can be several degrees hotter than the surrounding countryside, an effect known as the 'urban heat island'. Shade and water released from leaves both help to lower the temperature.

D
Critics point out that tiny forests are expensive to plant, because of the large number of saplings and the preparation of the soil. Others worry that too many fast-growing trees in a small space may not all survive. Supporters reply that even if some die, the forest as a whole still provides shelter for birds and insects in places where there was nothing before.

Read the article about an unusual museum, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

The museum of ordinary things

A
Most museums display treasures: gold jewellery, ancient swords, paintings by famous artists. A small museum in Peshawar does the opposite. Its glass cases hold a broken transistor radio, a school satchel from the 1970s, a set of tin cups and a bicycle bell. The founder, retired schoolteacher Gul Rehman, calls it 'a museum of everyday life'.

B
Gul began collecting thirty years ago, when he noticed that his neighbours were throwing away things their parents had used for decades. 'Nobody thought these objects mattered,' he says. 'But once they are gone, our grandchildren will have no idea how we lived.' Every item has a label explaining who owned it and how it was used.

C
Visitors react in surprising ways. Older people often stand in front of a cabinet for a long time, then start telling strangers about their own childhood. Gul now records these stories on his phone and has collected more than two hundred of them. Young visitors, meanwhile, are amazed that people once listened to cricket matches on the radio instead of watching them.

D
The museum survives on donations, and the building badly needs a new roof before the next monsoon. A university in the city has offered to help digitise the collection and the recorded stories, so that people around the world can explore them online. Gul is pleased, but insists that 'nothing replaces holding the real thing in your hands.'

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article

Read the article about saving water at home, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Every drop counts

A
In many cities, people only think about water when the taps run dry. Yet engineers warn that demand is growing faster than supply in much of South Asia, as populations rise and underground water levels fall. In some neighbourhoods, families already depend on water tankers for part of the year, paying far more per litre than those connected to the mains.

B
The good news, according to researchers who measured water use in two hundred homes, is that households waste far more than they realise. A single dripping tap can lose thousands of litres a year, and a leaking toilet cistern even more, often silently. 'Most families we visited had no idea they had a leak,' said one of the team. Simple repairs cost very little compared with the water saved.

C
Habits matter too, although changing them is harder. Washing a car with a bucket instead of a hose, or turning off the tap while brushing teeth, may seem trivial. But the researchers found that when families saw a weekly chart of their own water use, many cut their consumption without being asked, apparently motivated by comparing themselves with their neighbours.

D
Some experts argue that individual efforts, while welcome, cannot solve the problem on their own. Agriculture uses by far the largest share of water in the region, and old city pipes lose a large proportion of their supply before it reaches anyone's home. Real progress, they say, will need investment by governments as well as care from citizens.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article

Read the article about a runner with asthma, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Breathing room

A
As a child in Quetta, Mahnoor Baloch was the girl who sat on the bench during sports lessons. Cold, dry air brought on her asthma attacks, and her teachers, worried about her safety, rarely let her run. 'Everyone was very kind,' she remembers, 'but kindness can also keep you very small.'

B
Things changed when she was fifteen and saw a new doctor, who adjusted her medicine and explained that, for most people, asthma that is well controlled need not stop them exercising. He suggested she start with short, gentle runs and always warm up slowly. Mahnoor was sceptical. 'I'd spent ten years being told the opposite,' she says.

C
The early months were discouraging. She could barely jog for five minutes, and on windy days she had to stop completely. She kept a diary of every run, noting the weather and how her breathing felt, and gradually noticed patterns: early mornings in winter were the worst, while warm, humid evenings were easiest.

D
Eight years later, Mahnoor has completed three marathons and now coaches a running group for teenagers with breathing conditions. She is careful not to promise too much. 'Asthma is different for everyone,' she tells them, 'and you must work with your doctor. But don't let other people decide what your body can do.'
