practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Nida Hassan, who presents the weather forecast on television. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Nida, did you always want to work on television?
Nida: Not at all! I studied physics and then meteorology, the science of weather. I was working at the weather office, preparing forecasts, when the TV station asked for someone to present them. I was terrified at first.
Interviewer: How is a forecast prepared?
Nida: We use information from satellites, weather balloons and stations all over the country. Computers turn this into predictions, but forecasters still check them, because the computer can make mistakes, especially in the mountains.
Interviewer: What's the hardest weather to predict?
Nida: Thunderstorms. They can form very quickly over a small area, so one town gets heavy rain and the next stays dry.
Interviewer: Do people complain when you're wrong?
Nida: Of course! But the forecast for the next day is right about nine times out of ten now – much better than when I started.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What was Nida doing before she worked on television?
A preparing forecasts at the weather office
B teaching physics
C studying journalism
parts.answer: A preparing forecasts at the weather office
parts.working: She was working at the weather office, preparing forecasts.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Why do forecasters check the computer's predictions?
A Viewers ask them to.
B Satellites sometimes stop working.
C The computer can make mistakes.
parts.answer: C The computer can make mistakes.
parts.working: 'The computer can make mistakes, especially in the mountains.'

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Why are thunderstorms hard to predict?
A They happen mostly at night.
B They form quickly over small areas.
C They only happen in the mountains.
parts.answer: B They form quickly over small areas.
parts.working: They form quickly over a small area.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Ustad Ghulam Hussain, a craftsman who makes glazed tiles in Sindh. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Ustad sahib, your family has made tiles for generations. When did you start?
Ghulam Hussain: I was eight. In those days children learned by watching. My father never explained anything; he simply expected me to copy him. I made many mistakes, and he made me start again each time.
Interviewer: What makes your tiles special?
Ghulam Hussain: The blue colour. We make it from minerals, using a recipe that my family has kept secret for more than a century. Many people think it's the patterns that matter most, but anyone can copy a pattern. The colour is what customers recognise.
Interviewer: Is the craft in danger?
Ghulam Hussain: Factory-made tiles are cheaper, so fewer people buy handmade ones for their homes. Our main customers now are architects restoring old buildings, and some hotels. The real danger is that young people don't want to learn, because it takes years before you earn a good living.
Interviewer: Are you teaching anyone?
Ghulam Hussain: Two of my grandsons, and – for the first time in our family – my granddaughter. She is the most patient of all.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How did Ghulam Hussain learn his craft?
A He attended a training school.
B His father explained each step carefully.
C He copied his father and started again whenever he made a mistake.
parts.answer: C He copied his father and started again whenever he made a mistake.
parts.working: His father never explained; he expected him to copy and made him start again after mistakes.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
According to Ghulam Hussain, what makes his tiles special?
A the patterns
B the colour
C the low price
parts.working: 'The colour is what customers recognise.' He says anyone can copy a pattern.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What does he see as the greatest danger to the craft?
A cheaper factory tiles
B a lack of customers among architects
C young people not wanting to learn
parts.answer: C young people not wanting to learn
parts.working: 'The real danger is that young people don't want to learn.' Factory tiles are a problem but not called the real danger.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
What does he say about his granddaughter?
A She has started her own business.
B She designs new patterns.
C She is the most patient learner.
parts.answer: C She is the most patient learner.
parts.working: 'She is the most patient of all.'

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Dr Sameer Khan, the director of a planetarium. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Dr Khan, what exactly is a planetarium?
Dr Khan: It's a theatre with a dome-shaped ceiling. We project images of the night sky onto the dome, so visitors feel as if they're lying under the stars. We can show the sky from any place on earth, and even from the past or future.
Interviewer: Who are your visitors?
Dr Khan: Mainly school groups during the week. At weekends it's families. What's interesting is that adults often ask more questions than the children!
Interviewer: Has technology changed planetariums?
Dr Khan: Enormously. When I started, we used a huge mechanical projector with hundreds of tiny lenses. Now it's all digital, so we can fly visitors to Mars or inside a storm on Jupiter. Some people say the old shows were more beautiful, and I partly agree, but the digital shows are far more flexible.
Interviewer: What's your most popular show?
Dr Khan: We expected the show about black holes to be the favourite. In fact, it's one about how ancient travellers used the stars to find their way across deserts and oceans.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What does Dr Khan find interesting about visitors?
A Families prefer weekday visits.
B Adults often ask more questions than children.
C Children ask the most questions.
parts.answer: B Adults often ask more questions than children.
parts.working: 'Adults often ask more questions than the children!'

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What is Dr Khan's opinion of digital shows?
A They are more flexible than the old shows.
B They are less popular than the old shows.
C They are more beautiful than the old shows.
parts.answer: A They are more flexible than the old shows.
parts.working: He partly agrees the old shows were more beautiful but says digital shows are 'far more flexible'.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Which is the most popular show?
A a trip to Mars
B a show about navigating by the stars
C a show about black holes
parts.answer: B a show about navigating by the stars
parts.working: The show about how ancient travellers used the stars. Black holes were expected to be the favourite.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Tomás Ruiz, a cook on a research ship in the Southern Ocean. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Tomás, what's it like cooking on a ship?
Tomás: Challenging! When the waves are big, the whole kitchen moves. Every pot has to be fixed to the cooker with metal rails, and I never fill a pan more than half full.
Interviewer: How do you plan the food for a long trip?
Tomás: We're at sea for up to two months, with forty scientists and crew. I order everything before we leave. Fresh vegetables only last about three weeks, so after that it's frozen and tinned food. The thing people miss most isn't fruit, surprisingly – it's fresh milk.
Interviewer: Is food important for the people on board?
Tomás: Absolutely. The work is hard and the weather is grey for weeks. A good meal is the highlight of the day. On Sundays I cook something special, and on birthdays I always bake a cake, even in a storm.
Interviewer: Do you ever get seasick?
Tomás: I did on my first voyage. Now, after twelve years, never.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does Tomás never fill a pan more than half full?
A because the cooker is small
B because the ship moves
C to save food
parts.working: When waves are big the kitchen moves.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What do people on the ship miss most?
A fresh vegetables
B fresh milk
C fruit
parts.working: 'The thing people miss most isn't fruit, surprisingly – it's fresh milk.'

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What does Tomás say about his first voyage?
A He cooked a birthday cake in a storm.
B He ran out of food.
C He was seasick.
parts.working: 'I did [get seasick] on my first voyage.'

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Farida Noor, who translates children's books from English into Urdu. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Farida, is translating children's books easier than translating books for adults?
Farida: Many people think so, because the sentences are shorter. But it's often harder. Children's books are full of jokes, rhymes and word games, and these rarely work in another language. I sometimes spend a whole day on a single rhyme.
Interviewer: Do you ever change the stories?
Farida: I try not to change the plot. But I sometimes change small details, like food. If a character eats something Pakistani children have never heard of, I might change it to something familiar, so that the reader isn't confused.
Interviewer: How do you know if a translation is good?
Farida: I read it aloud to my nephews. If they get bored, I know something is wrong. Children are very honest critics – much more honest than editors!
Interviewer: Why is this work important?
Farida: Many children in Pakistan learn to read in Urdu first. If they can enjoy the same stories as children elsewhere, reading becomes a pleasure, not just schoolwork.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
According to Farida, why can children's books be hard to translate?
A Jokes and rhymes rarely work in another language.
B The sentences are very long.
C The plots are complicated.
parts.answer: A Jokes and rhymes rarely work in another language.
parts.working: Jokes, rhymes and word games rarely work in another language. She says sentences are shorter.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What does Farida sometimes change?
A small details such as food
B the ending
C the plot
parts.answer: A small details such as food
parts.working: She doesn't change the plot but changes small details like food.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
How does Farida test her translations?
A She reads them aloud to children.
B She compares them with other translations.
C She sends them to editors.
parts.answer: A She reads them aloud to children.
parts.working: She reads them aloud to her nephews.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Major (retired) Saad Rehman, a helicopter pilot who carries out mountain rescues. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Major Rehman, what's the most difficult part of a mountain rescue?
Saad: The altitude. Above about six thousand metres, the air is so thin that the helicopter's blades have very little to push against. We have to remove every unnecessary item, even seats, to make the machine lighter.
Interviewer: Who do you usually rescue?
Saad: Climbers who are injured or suffering from altitude sickness. But not always foreign climbers – we often rescue local porters, and sometimes villagers trapped by floods or landslides.
Interviewer: Do you ever have to say no?
Saad: Sadly, yes. Weather decides everything. If clouds cover the mountain or the wind is too strong, flying would put the crew in danger too. Waiting is the hardest part of the job, knowing someone is up there.
Interviewer: What advice would you give to climbers?
Saad: Turn back early. Most of the people we rescue kept going when their bodies were telling them to stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the crew remove items from the helicopter at high altitude?
A to make room for injured climbers
B to make the helicopter lighter
C to save fuel
parts.answer: B to make the helicopter lighter
parts.working: 'To make the machine lighter.'

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What does Saad find hardest about his job?
A waiting when it is too dangerous to fly
B rescuing local villagers
C flying in thin air
parts.answer: A waiting when it is too dangerous to fly
parts.working: 'Waiting is the hardest part of the job.'

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What is Saad's advice to climbers?
A Hire local porters.
B Turn back early.
C Check the weather forecast.
parts.working: 'Turn back early.'

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Dr Ayesha Siddiqa, a food scientist who works on mangoes. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Dr Siddiqa, what problem are you trying to solve?
Dr Siddiqa: Pakistan grows some of the best mangoes in the world, but a large share of the harvest is wasted before it reaches customers. Mangoes ripen quickly, and they're easily bruised on bumpy roads.
Interviewer: What have you discovered?
Dr Siddiqa: We've tested a natural coating made from plant wax. It slows down ripening, so the fruit stays firm for an extra week. Better packaging helps too – we use boxes with separate spaces for each mango, so they don't knock against each other.
Interviewer: Why does an extra week matter so much?
Dr Siddiqa: Because it means mangoes can be sent to other countries by sea instead of by air. Sea transport is much cheaper, so more farmers can afford to export.
Interviewer: Are farmers using the coating?
Dr Siddiqa: A few large farms are. Small farmers are interested, but they worry about the cost, so we're trying to make it cheaper.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is much of the mango harvest wasted?
A Customers prefer imported fruit.
B There are not enough workers to pick them.
C The mangoes ripen quickly and bruise easily.
parts.answer: C The mangoes ripen quickly and bruise easily.
parts.working: Mangoes ripen quickly and are easily bruised.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What is the main advantage of keeping mangoes firm for an extra week?
A They taste sweeter.
B They can be sent abroad by sea.
C They can be sold at a higher price in Pakistan.
parts.answer: B They can be sent abroad by sea.
parts.working: Mangoes can be sent by sea instead of by air.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Why are small farmers not yet using the coating?
A They do not believe it works.
B They do not grow enough mangoes.
C They are worried about the cost.
parts.answer: C They are worried about the cost.
parts.working: 'They worry about the cost.'

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Sana Yousuf, who teaches Pakistan Sign Language. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Sana, how did you become a sign language teacher?
Sana: My younger brother was born deaf. When I was small, our family communicated with him using simple gestures we invented ourselves. It was only when he started at a special school that we all learned proper sign language.
Interviewer: Who comes to your classes?
Sana: Mostly parents of deaf children, but also teachers, doctors and shop workers. Recently a bank sent all its customer service staff.
Interviewer: What do beginners find most difficult?
Sana: People expect the hand shapes to be hard, but they learn those quite quickly. What's harder is facial expression. In sign language, your face shows whether something is a question, or how strongly you feel. Many learners are shy about using their faces.
Interviewer: What would you like to change?
Sana: I'd like every school to teach some basic signs, so that deaf children can talk to their classmates during break.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How did Sana's family communicate with her brother at first?
A by writing notes
B using proper sign language
C using gestures they invented
parts.working: Simple gestures they invented themselves.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
According to Sana, what do beginners find most difficult?
A remembering vocabulary
B using facial expressions
C learning hand shapes
parts.working: Facial expression is harder; hand shapes are learned quickly.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What would Sana like schools to do?
A teach all pupils some basic signs
B employ more deaf teachers
C send teachers to her classes
parts.answer: A teach all pupils some basic signs
parts.working: She wants every school to teach some basic signs.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Bilal Ahmed, an architect who designs earthquake-resistant houses. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Bilal, why did you become interested in earthquake-safe buildings?
Bilal: I was a student in 2005 when the earthquake struck northern Pakistan. I volunteered in the affected area and saw that many deaths happened because heavy concrete roofs collapsed onto people.
Interviewer: What makes a building safe in an earthquake?
Bilal: It must be able to bend a little without breaking. Surprisingly, some traditional buildings did very well, because they used wooden frames filled with stone. Wood is flexible. My designs use that old idea, combined with modern materials.
Interviewer: Are safe houses more expensive?
Bilal: Slightly, maybe ten per cent more. But the real problem isn't cost, it's knowledge. Many builders in villages have never been trained, so we run free courses for them.
Interviewer: What's your biggest achievement?
Bilal: Last year, a moderate earthquake hit a valley where we had built two hundred homes. Not one of them was seriously damaged.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What did Bilal notice in 2005?
A Many deaths were caused by heavy roofs collapsing.
B Wooden houses burned down.
C There were not enough doctors.
parts.answer: A Many deaths were caused by heavy roofs collapsing.
parts.working: Heavy concrete roofs collapsed onto people.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Why did some traditional buildings survive well?
A They were built on rock.
B Their wooden frames were flexible.
C They had concrete roofs.
parts.answer: B Their wooden frames were flexible.
parts.working: Wood is flexible.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
According to Bilal, what is the main obstacle to building safer houses?
A the cost
B builders' lack of training
C a lack of materials
parts.working: 'The real problem isn't cost, it's knowledge.'

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Katie Moss, who rowed alone across the Atlantic Ocean. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Katie, you spent seventy-two days alone in a small boat. What was the hardest part?
Katie: Everyone expects me to say the storms or the loneliness. The storms were frightening, and I did feel lonely sometimes, but the hardest thing was sleep. I could only sleep for about ninety minutes at a time, because I had to keep checking the boat's direction.
Interviewer: What did you eat?
Katie: Mostly dried food that I mixed with seawater after it had been through a machine that removes the salt. By the end I never wanted to see another packet of dried pasta!
Interviewer: Did anything surprise you?
Katie: The wildlife. A group of dolphins swam beside me for two whole days. And I found plastic rubbish floating in the middle of the ocean, thousands of kilometres from land. That was shocking.
Interviewer: Would you do it again?
Katie: Not alone. Next time I'd like to row with a team, so that I can share the experience.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What does Katie say was the hardest part of the journey?
A feeling lonely
B not getting enough sleep
C the storms
parts.working: 'The hardest thing was sleep.'

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What shocked Katie?
A finding plastic in the middle of the ocean
B running out of food
C seeing dolphins
parts.answer: A finding plastic in the middle of the ocean
parts.working: Plastic thousands of kilometres from land was shocking. The dolphins were a pleasant surprise.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What does Katie plan to do in future?
A row with a team
B row alone again
C stop rowing
parts.working: 'Next time I'd like to row with a team.'

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Hamza Malik, who composes music for video games. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Hamza, how is writing music for games different from writing music for films?
Hamza: In a film, you know exactly what will happen and when. In a game, the player decides. So the music has to change depending on what the player does – it might become faster in a battle and calmer when they're exploring.
Interviewer: How did you get into this work?
Hamza: I studied classical piano, but I was always playing games. I started by making music for small games made by friends, without being paid. One of those games became popular, and a big company contacted me.
Interviewer: Do you use traditional instruments?
Hamza: Yes, in my last game I used the rubab and the dhol, recorded by musicians in Peshawar. Players from all over the world wrote to ask what those sounds were.
Interviewer: Any advice for young composers?
Hamza: Don't wait for permission. Make something, share it and keep learning.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How is game music different from film music, according to Hamza?
A It must change according to what the player does.
B It uses only electronic instruments.
C It is always faster.
parts.answer: A It must change according to what the player does.
parts.working: The music has to change depending on what the player does.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
How did Hamza get his first professional job?
A He won a competition.
B A game he worked on for friends became popular.
C He studied music at university.
parts.answer: B A game he worked on for friends became popular.
parts.working: One of the friends' games became popular and a big company contacted him.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What happened after Hamza used traditional instruments?
A The game was not popular.
B Musicians from Peshawar complained.
C Players asked about the sounds.
parts.answer: C Players asked about the sounds.
parts.working: Players from all over the world wrote to ask what the sounds were.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Dr Lucia Bianchi, a volcanologist who studies active volcanoes. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Dr Bianchi, what first attracted you to volcanoes?
Dr Bianchi: People assume it was the excitement – the red lava and so on. And yes, that's spectacular. But I was really drawn to the idea of prediction. My grandparents lost their farm in an eruption that no one saw coming, and I grew up wondering whether it could have been predicted.
Interviewer: And can eruptions be predicted?
Dr Bianchi: Better than before, though not perfectly. We measure small earthquakes under the volcano, changes in the gases coming out of it and tiny changes in the shape of the ground, which can swell as molten rock rises. No single sign is reliable on its own. It's when several change together that we get worried.
Interviewer: Is it dangerous work?
Dr Bianchi: It can be, but most of my time is spent in an office analysing data. The danger isn't really the lava, which usually moves slowly enough to walk away from. Clouds of hot gas and ash are far more deadly.
Interviewer: What's the hardest part of your job?
Dr Bianchi: Deciding when to advise people to leave their homes. If we warn too early and nothing happens, people stop trusting us next time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What was the main reason Dr Bianchi became interested in volcanoes?
A a wish to know whether eruptions can be predicted
B the excitement of seeing lava
C her grandparents worked as scientists
parts.answer: A a wish to know whether eruptions can be predicted
parts.working: She was drawn to the idea of prediction after her grandparents lost their farm. She admits lava is spectacular but says it wasn't the real reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What does she say about the signs that an eruption may happen?
A Small earthquakes are the most reliable sign.
B Changes in the ground are impossible to measure.
C Several signs changing together are most worrying.
parts.answer: C Several signs changing together are most worrying.
parts.working: 'No single sign is reliable on its own. It's when several change together that we get worried.'

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Why does Dr Bianchi find it hard to advise people to leave their homes?
A Lava moves too quickly to escape.
B There are not enough safe places to go.
C People may not trust future warnings if nothing happens.
parts.answer: C People may not trust future warnings if nothing happens.
parts.working: If they warn too early and nothing happens, people stop trusting them. She says lava usually moves slowly.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Dr Uzma Baig, a scientist who studies the Indus river dolphin. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Dr Baig, what makes the Indus river dolphin unusual?
Dr Baig: It lives only in the Indus River system, and it's almost blind. The river water is so muddy that eyesight is of little use, so it finds its way and catches fish using echolocation – it sends out clicks and listens to the echoes.
Interviewer: Are its numbers increasing or falling?
Dr Baig: The good news is that they've risen in recent decades, thanks to protection and to fishermen who now help rather than harm them. But I wouldn't say the dolphin is safe. Its range is much smaller than it once was.
Interviewer: What's the biggest threat today?
Dr Baig: Many people say pollution, and that is a concern. But the most serious problem is the barrages – the dams built across the river for irrigation. They split the dolphins into separate groups, and in the dry season, some sections hold so little water that dolphins become trapped in canals.
Interviewer: What happens then?
Dr Baig: We have a rescue team. Local people phone us, and we catch the dolphins in nets and carry them back to the main river. Last year we rescued over twenty.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the Indus river dolphin use echolocation?
A Its eyesight is useless in the muddy water.
B It hunts only at night.
C It lives in very deep water.
parts.answer: A Its eyesight is useless in the muddy water.
parts.working: The water is so muddy that eyesight is of little use.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
What is Dr Baig's view of the dolphin's situation?
A It is now completely safe.
B Numbers have improved, but it is not yet safe.
C Numbers are falling quickly.
parts.answer: B Numbers have improved, but it is not yet safe.
parts.working: Numbers have risen, 'but I wouldn't say the dolphin is safe'.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What does Dr Baig consider the most serious threat?
A pollution
B fishermen
C barrages across the river
parts.working: 'The most serious problem is the barrages.' Pollution is a concern but not the most serious; fishermen now help.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Professor Nadeem Akhtar, an archaeologist who has worked at Mohenjo-daro. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Professor Akhtar, what still amazes you about Mohenjo-daro?
Professor Akhtar: The planning. More than four thousand years ago, the city had straight streets, covered drains and houses with their own bathrooms. Many people focus on the Great Bath, which is impressive, but for me the drains are the real achievement – they tell us that the rulers cared about public health.
Interviewer: What don't we know about the city?
Professor Akhtar: A great deal. We can't read the writing of the Indus people. We have thousands of short inscriptions on small stone seals, but no long texts, and nothing like a dictionary. So we don't know what language they spoke or what they called their city.
Interviewer: Is the site in danger?
Professor Akhtar: Very much. The bricks are being damaged by salt rising from the ground water. When the water evaporates, salt crystals grow inside the bricks and break them apart. Tourists can cause damage too, by climbing on the walls, but salt is a far bigger threat.
Interviewer: Should more of the city be dug up?
Professor Akhtar: I'd say no, at least for now. Buried parts are protected. Once they're exposed, they start to decay. Better to look after what we've already uncovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What does Professor Akhtar consider the city's greatest achievement?
A the drains
B the Great Bath
C the writing on seals
parts.working: 'For me the drains are the real achievement.' The Great Bath is impressive but not his choice.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Why can't scholars read the Indus writing?
A The seals are too small to see.
B All the inscriptions have been destroyed.
C There are no long texts or anything like a dictionary.
parts.answer: C There are no long texts or anything like a dictionary.
parts.working: Only short inscriptions, no long texts, no dictionary.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
What is his opinion about digging up more of the city?
A It should wait, because buried parts are protected.
B It should be done as soon as possible.
C It should be done only by tourists' guides.
parts.answer: A It should wait, because buried parts are protected.
parts.working: He says no for now: buried parts are protected and exposed parts decay.

practice.stem:
You will hear an interview with Dr Rehana Qazi, a neuroscientist who studies memory. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Dr Qazi, many students believe they have a bad memory. Is that true?
Dr Qazi: Usually not. Most people who say that simply use poor methods. Reading notes again and again feels productive, but it's one of the least effective ways to learn. Testing yourself is far better, even if you get answers wrong.
Interviewer: Why does testing work?
Dr Qazi: Every time you try to recall something, you strengthen the connections in your brain that hold that memory. Getting it wrong and then checking also helps, because the correction sticks.
Interviewer: What about sleep?

Dr Qazi: They make you better at that particular game. There's little evidence they improve memory in general. Physical exercise, surprisingly, has a much clearer effect.

Bringing nature indoors
Houseplants have become hugely popular in recent years, especially among young people living in small city flats. Shops that once sold only a few spider plants now offer hundreds of different kinds.

Ready for exams
Exams are stressful for almost every student, but good preparation can make a huge difference. Teachers and psychologists agree on several simple steps.

practice.stem:
Read the article about the decline of house sparrows in cities, and then answer the question.

Where have the sparrows gone?
Not long ago, the cheerful chirping of house sparrows was one of the most familiar sounds in towns across South Asia. Sparrows nested in the roofs of houses, hopped around market stalls and bathed in the dust at the side of the road. In many cities today, however, they have become hard to find. Scientists have suggested several reasons for their decline.
One major cause is the change in buildings. Older houses had gaps under roof tiles and holes in walls where sparrows could build their nests, but modern concrete and glass buildings offer no such spaces. At the same time, gardens and empty plots of land, where sparrows once found seeds and insects, have been replaced by car parks and roads.
Changes in shopping have also played a part. In the past, grain was sold loose from open sacks, and sparrows could pick up what was spilled. Now most food is sold in sealed plastic packets. Sparrows also like to clean their feathers by bathing in dust, but the bare patches of earth they used have mostly been covered with concrete and paving.
Young sparrows are fed almost entirely on insects in their first days, but the use of chemical pesticides in parks and gardens has reduced the number of insects available. Some researchers believe that air pollution from traffic may also harm the birds' health, although this has not yet been proved. Finally, cities now have large numbers of crows and pet cats, which take sparrows' eggs and chicks.
Bird lovers in several cities have started putting up wooden nest boxes and bowls of water, and in some neighbourhoods sparrows are slowly returning. March 20th is now celebrated as World Sparrow Day.

Moving to the big city
Every year, hundreds of thousands of people in Pakistan move from villages and small towns to big cities such as Karachi, Lahore and Faisalabad. Most come in search of work or education. For many, though, the first months are much harder than they expected.

practice.stem:
Read the article about traditional ways of preserving food, and then answer the question.

Keeping food before fridges
Refrigerators have only been common in homes for around a hundred years, and in many villages they are still a luxury. So how did people keep food from going bad in the past? The answer is a range of clever methods, many of which are still used today.
Drying is one of the oldest. Fruit such as apricots and dates, as well as fish and meat, were spread out in the sun until most of the water had gone, because bacteria cannot grow easily without water. In the mountains of northern Pakistan, dried apricots are still an important winter food.
Salt was also widely used. Packing fish or meat in salt draws water out of it and prevents bacteria from growing. Sugar works in a similar way, which is why fruit can be kept for months as jam. Milk, which goes sour within hours in hot weather, was often turned into ghee, which keeps for months.
In South Asia, pickling in oil, vinegar and spices was – and still is – a popular method. Mango and lemon pickles can last for a year or more. Smoking meat or fish over a wood fire both dries it and adds substances that slow down decay.
To keep water and milk cool, people used clay pots, which allow a little water to seep through and evaporate, cooling the contents. Some households stored food in underground rooms or in cool streams.
Many people say that food preserved in these ways has a richer flavour than anything kept in a fridge.

Too loud to live with
Car horns, rickshaw engines, construction machines, wedding loudspeakers: for people living in many cities, noise never really stops. Doctors now say that this constant noise is not just annoying but harmful to health.
The most obvious effect is damage to hearing. People exposed to very loud noise for long periods, such as workers in factories or traffic police at busy junctions, may gradually lose their hearing, and the damage is often permanent. Some also develop a constant ringing in the ears.
Noise also disturbs sleep. Even if people do not wake up completely, noise at night can stop them from sleeping deeply, leaving them tired and irritable the next day. Over time, this lack of sleep can weaken the immune system.
Studies have found that people living near busy roads or airports are more likely to suffer from high blood pressure and heart disease, because noise causes the body to release stress hormones. Children in noisy schools may find it harder to concentrate, read and remember information. Noise can also increase anxiety and make people more likely to argue with each other.
Experts recommend planting trees along roads, using double-glazed windows and enforcing laws against unnecessary use of horns.

practice.stem:
Read the article about how desert animals cope with heat, and then answer the question.

Surviving the furnace
In the Thar and Cholistan deserts, summer temperatures can rise above 45 °C, and rain may not fall for months. Yet these deserts are home to a surprising variety of animals. Over thousands of years, they have developed different ways of coping with the heat.
Many desert animals simply avoid the hottest part of the day. Desert foxes, gerbils and many snakes are nocturnal: they rest in underground burrows during the day, where the temperature is much lower, and come out to hunt or feed at night when the air has cooled.
Some animals lose heat through their bodies. Desert hares and foxes have large ears full of blood vessels; as blood passes through them, heat escapes into the air. Pale fur or skin reflects sunlight, helping animals to stay cooler.
Saving water is equally important. Some small rodents rarely drink at all; they get most of the water they need from seeds and plants, and their bodies produce very concentrated urine so that little water is lost. The camel can go for days without drinking, and its body temperature is allowed to rise during the day so that it sweats less, saving water.
Lizards control their temperature by changing their position, moving between sun and shade and sometimes lifting their feet off the hot sand one at a time.
Scientists warn that as the climate gets hotter, even these well-adapted animals may struggle to survive.

In the narrow lanes of Anarkali Bazaar in Lahore, hundreds of small shops sell almost identical goods: bangles, shawls, shoes and spices. Some are always busy, while others nearby stand almost empty. What makes the difference?
Shopkeeper Javed Akhtar, who has sold shawls in the same spot for thirty years, believes the most important factor is trust. Younger shopkeepers have added modern ideas. Many now accept mobile payments, which tourists and young customers prefer, and some advertise new stock on social media and offer home delivery. Others work with nearby shops, sending customers to a neighbour who has what they need – knowing that the favour will be returned.
Javed admits that location helps: shops near the main entrance get more passing customers. 'But a good shop in a bad place,' he says, 'will still beat a bad shop in a good place.'

Why Lahore can't breathe
Every year, from late October until January, a thick grey haze settles over Lahore and much of Punjab. On the worst days, buildings a few hundred metres away disappear from view, schools close and hospitals fill with people suffering from coughs and breathing problems. Scientists say there is no single cause of the smog; instead, several sources of pollution combine with the winter weather.
Vehicles are one of the largest sources. The number of cars, motorbikes and rickshaws in Lahore has grown rapidly, and many older vehicles, as well as some fuel of poor quality, release large amounts of smoke and harmful gases.
Industry adds to the problem. Factories on the edge of the city burn coal, oil and sometimes waste materials such as old tyres. Hundreds of traditional brick kilns around the city burn fuel inefficiently and produce thick black smoke.
At the start of winter, farmers in Punjab – on both sides of the border – burn the stubble left in their fields after the rice harvest, because it is the quickest and cheapest way to clear the land for the next crop. The smoke drifts towards the cities.
Dust from building sites and unpaved roads, and the burning of rubbish in the open, add further pollution.
Finally, the weather traps all of this close to the ground. In winter, the wind is often very light, and a layer of warm air above the city can act like a lid, preventing pollution from rising and spreading out.
The government has tried several measures, including closing kilns and schools on the worst days, but experts say lasting improvement will need action on every source at once.

Growing food above the city
In Karachi, more and more families are turning the flat roofs of their houses into small vegetable gardens. Saima Qureshi, a retired teacher in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, started with three plastic buckets of tomatoes. Today her roof has twenty containers of chillies, spinach, mint and bitter gourd.
Saima says the biggest benefit is the money she saves. 'Vegetable prices go up every month, but my spinach costs me almost nothing,' she explains. She also knows exactly what is in her food, because she uses no chemical sprays. The plants have another effect, too: the leaves shade the concrete, so the rooms below stay noticeably cooler in summer.
Rooftop gardening is not always easy, however. Water is the main difficulty, because the city often has shortages and plants on a hot roof dry out quickly. Saima collects the water she uses for washing vegetables and pours it on her plants. Strong sea winds can also break young plants, so she ties them to wooden sticks. Pests are a further problem: pigeons and crows peck at ripe tomatoes, so she covers them with old fishing nets. Finally, soil is heavy, and some older roofs cannot carry the weight of many large pots. Saima advises beginners to ask a builder to check their roof before they start.

It's never too late to swim

Instructors at a sports centre in Manchester say that fear of looking silly in front of others is the most common reason adults stay away from the pool. Others had a frightening experience in water when they were young, such as falling into a river. A third group simply believe that they are too old to learn a new physical skill.

Sunlight that pumps water
For generations, farmers in southern Punjab have used diesel engines to pump water from underground for their wheat and cotton fields. In the last few years, however, thousands have replaced their engines with solar-powered pumps.
Farmer Allah Ditta explains why he changed. 'Diesel was eating my profits. Once the solar panels were paid for, the sunlight was free.' Solar pumps are also much quieter, and there is no smoke, so the air around the village is cleaner. Because the pumps have few moving parts, they rarely break down, and Allah Ditta no longer has to travel to the nearest town for spare parts.

On cloudy days in the winter, the pumps produce much less water. A more serious concern is that, since pumping now costs nothing, some farmers leave their pumps running all day. Experts warn that the level of underground water is falling quickly in some districts. Theft is another worry: panels left in open fields have been stolen at night, so some farmers now pay guards.

In the Netherlands, around three-quarters of secondary school students cycle to school, often riding ten kilometres or more each way. Why is cycling so popular?
The country is almost completely flat, so even long journeys need little effort. Children are taught to cycle safely from an early age, and most take a practical cycling test at primary school. Bicycles are also cheaper than buses or cars over time, and parents like the fact that their children get exercise every day. Where have all the bees gone?
Bees pollinate around a third of the crops we eat, from apples to almonds. Yet in many parts of the world, bee numbers have fallen sharply in recent decades.
Scientists believe several factors are to blame. Certain pesticides used on crops can confuse bees so that they cannot find their way back to the hive. As farms grow larger and plant just one crop, bees lose the variety of flowers they need through the year. Hedges and wild meadows, where bees once nested, have been cleared for building. Why teenagers are always tired
Parents often complain that their teenage children stay up late and then cannot get out of bed in the morning. It is easy to call this laziness, but research tells a different story. During the teenage years, the body releases melatonin, the chemical that makes us sleepy, about two hours later than it does in childhood. A fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at ten o'clock may simply lie awake.
Modern habits make the problem worse. The blue light from phone and laptop screens delays sleep even further, and messages arriving late at night keep the brain alert. Many students also drink tea, coffee or energy drinks in the afternoon to get through homework, not realising that caffeine stays in the body for up to six hours. Heavy homework loads, of course, also push bedtime later.
What can be done? Although schools could help by starting later, there is a lot that teenagers can do themselves. Switching off screens an hour before bed is the single most effective step. Keeping the same wake-up time at weekends, rather than sleeping until noon, helps the body clock settle. A cool, dark bedroom also makes a difference. Finally, a short walk in daylight soon after waking tells the body that the day has begun.

Rainforests of the sea
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet scientists estimate that around a quarter of all sea creatures depend on them at some point in their lives. Young fish shelter among the corals before moving out to open water, which means that reefs support fisheries far beyond their own boundaries.
Reefs matter to people as well as to fish. They act like natural sea walls, breaking up powerful waves before they reach the shore and so protecting coastal villages from storms. Tourists travel across the world to dive and snorkel among the bright corals, bringing income to island nations. Medical researchers have also found substances in reef animals that are being tested as possible treatments for diseases.
Sadly, reefs are in danger. When sea temperatures rise even slightly, corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them and give them their colour. This process, known as bleaching, leaves the coral white and, if the heat continues, it dies. Pollution from farms washes fertilisers into the sea, which encourages seaweed to grow over the coral. Overfishing removes the fish that would normally eat this seaweed. In some places, careless divers and boat anchors break off pieces of coral that may have taken hundreds of years to grow.

Why cities are hotter than the countryside
On a summer evening, the centre of a large city such as Lahore or Delhi can be several degrees hotter than the farmland just outside it. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect.
Several features of cities produce this extra heat. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and black roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night, so the city never cools down properly. Tall buildings close together trap warm air and block the breeze. Cities also have fewer trees and fields, and so there is less water evaporating from leaves to cool the air. On top of this, air conditioners, vehicles and factories all give off heat directly into the streets.
Fortunately, there are practical solutions. Painting roofs white or light grey reflects much of the sunlight back into the sky; in some trials, this lowered the temperature inside top-floor rooms by several degrees. Planting trees along streets provides shade and cools the air, and small parks spread across a city are more effective than one large park on the edge. Some cities are replacing ordinary paving with materials that let rainwater soak through, which keeps the ground damp and cooler. Planners can also design wider streets that allow wind to flow through.

Strings attached
Hamza Siddiqui was nine when he first held a sitar. Now nineteen, he performs at concerts in Lahore and abroad. But he admits that the early years were hard.
'The sitar is not a friendly instrument for beginners,' he laughs. 'You have to sit cross-legged on the floor with the instrument balanced at an angle, and after twenty minutes my legs went numb.' When grasshoppers become an army
Most of the time, the desert locust is a harmless, solitary insect, living quietly in the dry lands between West Africa and India. Yet in the right conditions it changes into one of the most destructive pests on Earth, forming swarms that can contain billions of insects and travel over a hundred kilometres in a day.
The change begins with rain. Unusually heavy rainfall in the desert produces fresh plants, giving the locusts plenty of food and damp sand in which to lay eggs. Numbers rise rapidly. As the vegetation dries up again, the insects are forced together into the few green areas that remain. Being crowded causes a chemical change: their colour turns from green to yellow and black, and they start to seek each other out instead of avoiding each other. Winds then carry the young swarms towards farmland.
Controlling swarms is difficult and expensive. The main method is spraying chemical pesticides from aircraft or vehicles, ideally before the young locusts can fly. Some countries now use a natural fungus that kills locusts but is harmless to other animals. Satellite images help scientists predict where rain has fallen and where outbreaks are likely, so teams can be sent early. In Pakistan in 2020, farmers were even paid to collect locusts at night, which were then sold as chicken feed.

Guardians of the delta
Where the River Indus meets the Arabian Sea, the muddy coastline is fringed with mangrove forests. These unusual trees can survive in salty water, and their tangled roots rise above the mud like stilts.
Mangroves bring many benefits. Their roots slow down waves, protecting coastal settlements from storms and cyclones and preventing the shoreline from being washed away. The calm water among the roots is a nursery for shrimps, crabs and young fish, on which local fishing families depend. Mangroves also absorb large amounts of carbon dioxide from the air and store it in the mud, which helps to limit climate change. Camels are grazed on their leaves, and the forests attract birdwatchers.
For decades, the mangroves shrank because less fresh water reached the delta and people cut the trees for firewood. More recently, a major replanting effort has reversed some of this loss. Workers collect seeds from healthy trees and grow them in nurseries before planting the young trees in the mud at low tide. Local people are employed as forest guards to stop illegal cutting, and families are offered gas cookers so that they no longer need firewood. Schools organise planting days to teach children why mangroves matter.

You are preparing a presentation on natural hazards. Read this article about glacier lakes. Then complete the notes below. Write one short note on each bullet point. Your notes should be brief, and must come from the text.

The lakes that can burst
High in the mountains of northern Pakistan, rising temperatures are causing glaciers to melt faster than ever. The meltwater collects in lakes held back by walls of loose rock and ice. When these natural walls give way, a glacial lake outburst flood can send millions of tonnes of water rushing down the valley in minutes.
The dangers are severe. The floods carry boulders the size of cars, which destroy bridges and cut off villages from the outside world for weeks. Fields and orchards are buried under mud and stones, so families lose not only this year's harvest but their land for years to come. Water channels used for drinking water and irrigation are blocked. Because the floods happen so suddenly, people have very little time to escape.
To reduce the risk, communities have been working with scientists on early warning systems. Sensors placed near dangerous lakes measure the water level and send an alarm by mobile network if it rises quickly. Weather stations record temperature and rainfall, helping experts predict when an outburst is most likely. Villagers have been trained to act as volunteers who check the lakes and sound sirens. Safe meeting places on higher ground have been marked, and schools hold regular practice evacuations.

practice.stem:
You are entering a science fair. Read this advice from a teacher who has judged many competitions. Then complete the notes below. Write one short note on each bullet point. Your notes should be brief, and must come from the text.

How to impress the science fair judges
Every year I judge more than a hundred science fair projects, and the best ones are rarely the most expensive. What matters most is the thinking behind them.
Choosing the right topic is half the battle. Start with a question that genuinely interests you, because you will spend weeks on it. Make sure it is something you can actually test with equipment available at school or home; 'Does salt water freeze more slowly than tap water?' is far better than 'How can we stop climate change?'. Check that the experiment can be repeated several times in the time you have, since a single result proves very little. Avoid projects that simply copy instructions from a kit, as judges recognise these immediately.
Presentation is the other half. Your display board should be readable from two metres away, with large headings and clear graphs rather than long paragraphs. Be honest about results that did not go as expected; explaining why is a sign of a real scientist. Practise a two-minute summary of your project so that you can speak confidently when the judges arrive, and be ready to describe what you would do differently next time.

You are writing an article about railways for a transport magazine. Read this text. Then complete the notes below. Write one short note on each bullet point. Your notes should be brief, and must come from the text.

The trains that are never late
Japan's high-speed Shinkansen, often called the bullet train, began running in 1964. Since then it has carried billions of passengers, and the average delay is measured in seconds rather than minutes.
The trains have several remarkable features. Their long, pointed noses reduce the loud bang that older trains made when they entered tunnels at speed. The trains run on their own tracks, separate from slower local and goods trains. Earthquake sensors along the line can cut the power automatically, bringing every train to a stop within seconds if a tremor is detected. Inside, the seats can be turned around so that passengers always face the direction of travel.
Why are they so punctual? Part of the answer is careful planning: timetables are worked out to the quarter-minute, and drivers point at and call out every signal to avoid mistakes. Cleaning teams can clean an entire train in just seven minutes at the end of the line. Maintenance takes place every night after the last train, when the tracks are inspected inch by inch. Staff also see punctuality as a matter of personal pride, and a delay of even one minute is officially reported and investigated.

Speaker 5: Studying Japanese, I found that some words have no English translation, because they describe ideas special to Japanese life. It changed how I see the way people there think and behave.
Speaker 6: I got my job at an international hotel mainly because I can speak Spanish and Chinese as well as English. Companies everywhere are looking for people who speak more than one language.

You will hear six people talking about taking a gap year between school and university. For Speakers 1 to 6, choose from the list A–H which opinion each speaker expresses. Use each letter only once. There are two extra letters which you do not need to use.

A A gap year should be used to earn money.
B Travelling teaches you more than any classroom.
C Students may lose the habit of studying.
D A gap year needs careful planning to be useful.
E Employers value the experience gained.
F Parents worry too much about gap years.
G It is a chance to discover what you really want to study.
H Gap years are only possible for wealthy families.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Speaker 1: I spent my year working in a hospital laboratory, not travelling. I'd always assumed I'd do medicine, but seeing the work up close made me realise that research, not treating patients, was what excited me. I switched to biochemistry, and I've never regretted it.
Speaker 2: My friend took a year off and did nothing much – slept late, played games. When he finally started university he struggled to sit down with a textbook again. I'm not against gap years, but there's a real risk you forget how to concentrate on academic work.
Speaker 3: When I applied for jobs after graduating, every interviewer wanted to hear about my year teaching English in Indonesia. They said it showed I could cope with challenges and work with different people. I'm convinced it got me my first job.

Speaker 5: Of course I learned things travelling around South America, but I'd say the same about university. The point is, not everyone can afford flights and hostels. Unless your parents can pay, the gap year just isn't an option, which I think is unfair.

You will hear six people talking about working from home. For Speakers 1 to 6, choose from the list A–H which opinion each speaker expresses. Use each letter only once. There are two extra letters which you do not need to use.

A Working from home makes it hard to separate work and family life.
B Working from home is better for the environment.
C Managers find it difficult to trust staff they cannot see.
D Home workers miss the ideas that come from casual conversations.
E Working from home increases productivity.
F The best arrangement is a mix of home and office.
G Home working requires good self-discipline.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Speaker 1: Since our office went online, my laptop sits on the dining table. My children see me there and want to talk, and at nine at night I'm still answering emails. There's no moment when work stops and home begins.
Speaker 2: I enjoy the peace at home and I certainly don't miss the two-hour commute. But I'll admit something is lost. Some of our best product ideas used to start with a chat by the coffee machine, and you just don't get those chance conversations on a video call.
Speaker 3: Full-time at home, I felt isolated; full-time in the office, I was exhausted by travelling. Now I go in on Mondays and Thursdays and stay home the rest of the week. That balance suits me and my team perfectly.
Speaker 4: People think home working is a holiday. In fact, you have to be very strict with yourself – set an alarm, get dressed, plan your tasks for the day, and ignore the television. Without that, nothing gets done.
Speaker 5: My office colleagues can work from home, but I'm a nurse – I can't look after patients from my sofa. Neither can shop staff, bus drivers or factory workers. Somehow they're expected to keep travelling while others enjoy the freedom. It doesn't seem right.
Speaker 6: I run a team of twelve. Honestly, their output has gone up since they started working from home – reports are finished faster than before. I was worried at first that I'd have no idea what they were doing, but the results speak for themselves.

Speaker 4: I visited a garment factory as a journalist. Workers were sewing for twelve hours a day for wages they could barely live on, in buildings that weren't safe. Every time I see a very cheap shirt, I think of them.
Speaker 5: The companies make billions selling clothes. When those clothes end up in landfill, it's taxpayers who pay to deal with the waste. The brands should be made to fund collection and recycling schemes.
Speaker 6: When something costs less than a sandwich, nobody feels bad about wearing it twice and throwing it away. We've lost the idea that a shirt is something to keep for years.

You will hear a talk about the history of chocolate. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows only in hot, wet regions near the equator. The seeds, often called beans, grow inside large pods that sprout directly from the tree's trunk.
Some of the earliest people to use cacao lived in Central America thousands of years ago. The Maya and later the Aztecs made a drink from ground cacao beans mixed with water and chilli. It was bitter, not sweet, and was usually drunk by rulers and warriors. Cacao beans were so valuable that the Aztecs used them as money.
Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century. Europeans added sugar and later milk, and drinking chocolate became fashionable among the rich. Solid chocolate bars only appeared in the nineteenth century, when new machines made it possible to press cacao into a smooth, solid form.
Today, most of the world's cacao is grown not in the Americas but in West Africa, especially Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Many cacao farmers earn very little, and some people choose to buy chocolate with a Fairtrade label, which aims to guarantee farmers a fairer price.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Camels are perfectly designed for life in the desert. Many people think a camel's hump is full of water, but in fact it stores fat. When food is scarce, the camel's body uses this fat for energy, and the hump becomes smaller and floppy.
Camels can go for many days without drinking, partly because they lose very little water. They hardly sweat, even in great heat, and they produce dry droppings. When they do find water, they can drink an enormous amount very quickly.
Their bodies are protected from sand in clever ways. They have two rows of long eyelashes, and they can close their nostrils during sandstorms. Their wide, soft feet spread out on the sand, so they don't sink.
There are two main kinds of camel. The dromedary, found in South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, has one hump. The Bactrian camel, from the cold deserts of Central Asia, has two humps and grows a thick coat in winter.
In Thar and Cholistan, camels are still used to carry goods and water, and their milk is an important food for desert families. In recent years, camel milk has also become popular in cities because it contains about three times as much vitamin C as cow's milk.

Only free Greek men could compete. Women were not allowed to compete, and married women could not even watch, although they held their own separate games in honour of the goddess Hera. Winners did not receive medals; instead they were given a crown made of olive leaves.

The famous Olympic symbol of five rings was designed by Coubertin. The rings represent the five inhabited continents joined together. The Olympic flame is lit in Olympia using the sun's rays and then carried by runners to the host city.
Pakistan has had its greatest Olympic success in field hockey, winning gold medals three times.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Houseplants make rooms more attractive and can improve your mood, but many people kill them by mistake. The most common cause of death is not forgetting to water them, but watering too much. When soil stays wet all the time, the roots can't breathe and they begin to rot. A simple test is to push your finger into the soil: if the top two centimetres feel dry, it's time to water.
Always use pots with holes in the bottom, so that extra water can drain away. Put a saucer underneath to protect your furniture.
Light is the next thing to consider. Most houseplants come from tropical forests, where they grow in the shade of taller trees, so they prefer bright but indirect light. Strong afternoon sun through a window can burn their leaves.
In winter, plants grow more slowly and need less water. Keep them away from heaters, which dry the air.
If you're a beginner, start with an easy plant. The snake plant and the money plant are both very forgiving. They can survive in low light, and they won't die if you forget them for a couple of weeks.
Finally, wipe dusty leaves with a damp cloth now and then. Dust blocks light and stops the plant from making food.

The Indus River dolphin is one of the rarest freshwater dolphins in the world, and it's found almost entirely in Pakistan, in the Indus River; only a tiny group survives across the border in India. Locally it's called 'bhulan'.
This dolphin has a very unusual feature: it is almost completely blind. The muddy water of the Indus makes eyesight almost useless, so the dolphin finds its way and catches fish using echolocation. It sends out clicking sounds and listens for the echoes that bounce back.
Another strange habit is that it often swims on its side, with one flipper touching the river bed, which helps it search for food.

The good news is that numbers have increased in recent decades, thanks to protection laws and rescue teams who return stranded dolphins to the main river. A protected area called the Indus Dolphin Reserve has been created between the Sukkur and Guddu barrages, where most of the dolphins live.

You will hear a talk about volcanoes. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust through which molten rock, gases and ash escape. Molten rock underground is called magma; once it reaches the surface, it's called lava.
Most volcanoes are found where the Earth's tectonic plates meet. Around the Pacific Ocean there is a huge chain of volcanoes known as the Ring of Fire, where around three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes are located.
Not all eruptions are the same. Some volcanoes, such as those in Hawaii, produce runny lava that flows gently, and people can often watch from a safe distance. Others are much more explosive. When magma is thick and full of gas, pressure builds up until the volcano blows apart, throwing ash high into the atmosphere.
Ash is often more dangerous than lava. It can travel hundreds of kilometres, damage aircraft engines and collapse roofs under its weight. Fast-moving clouds of hot gas and ash, called pyroclastic flows, are the deadliest of all.
Despite the dangers, millions of people live near volcanoes, because volcanic soil is extremely fertile. Volcanoes also provide geothermal energy: in countries like Iceland, heat from underground is used to produce electricity and warm homes.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
When we watch a film, we rarely think about the sound. Yet much of what we hear wasn't recorded at the same time as the pictures. The dialogue is usually recorded on set, but noisy locations often make it unclear, so actors later go into a studio and repeat their lines while watching the film. This process is called dubbing, or ADR.
Then there are sound effects. Many everyday noises, like footsteps, doors closing or clothes rustling, are created by specialists called Foley artists, named after a sound pioneer, Jack Foley. They work in a studio full of strange objects. For example, the sound of someone walking through snow is often made by squeezing a bag of cornflour. Breaking celery can sound like bones breaking — useful for action films!
Background sound, known as 'ambience', is also important. A scene in a busy market needs distant voices, traffic and birds to feel real, even if the street was empty during filming.
Finally, all these layers are combined in a process called mixing. The engineer decides how loud each sound should be, so that the dialogue remains clear and the music supports the emotion of the scene without drowning it out.

You will hear a talk about the science of laughter. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
We usually think of laughter as a response to jokes, but researchers have found that most laughter has nothing to do with humour. In one study, scientists listened to people's everyday conversations and found that most laughs followed ordinary comments like 'See you later' rather than anything funny. Laughter, it seems, is mainly a social signal: it shows that we like someone and feel relaxed with them.
In fact, we're about thirty times more likely to laugh when we're with other people than when we're alone. Laughter is also contagious; hearing someone laugh activates areas of our brain that prepare us to join in. That's why some TV comedies use recorded laughter.
Laughter isn't only human. Chimpanzees and gorillas make a panting sound when they play and tickle each other, and researchers have even recorded rats making high-pitched chirps when tickled.
There are health benefits, too. A good laugh relaxes the muscles and may reduce stress hormones. Some hospitals now invite clowns to visit children's wards, and studies suggest this can reduce children's anxiety before operations.
However, laughter can also exclude people. Laughing at someone, rather than with them, can be a powerful way of showing who belongs to a group and who doesn't.

The Karakoram Highway is one of the highest paved international roads in the world. It connects Pakistan with China, crossing the border at the Khunjerab Pass, at a height of almost four thousand seven hundred metres.
The road was built jointly by Pakistan and China and was completed in the late 1970s after about twenty years of work. Building it was extremely dangerous. Workers had to cut through solid rock, often hanging from ropes on steep cliffs, and many lost their lives in landslides and accidents.
The highway follows ancient routes once used by traders on the Silk Road. Near the town of Chilas, you can still see thousands of rock carvings left by travellers and pilgrims over many centuries, showing animals, people and Buddhist symbols.
The road passes through some of the most dramatic scenery on Earth. It runs alongside the Indus and Hunza rivers and gives views of mountains such as Rakaposhi.
The highway has brought big changes to the region. Fruit such as apricots and cherries can now reach markets in the cities quickly, and tourism has grown. However, landslides still block the road regularly, especially after heavy rain, and in 2010 a huge landslide created a lake, Attabad Lake, which flooded part of the road.

You will hear a talk about sleep in animals. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
All animals that have been carefully studied seem to need some form of sleep, but the ways they do it vary enormously.
Dolphins face a special problem: they need to breathe air, so they can't become completely unconscious underwater. Their solution is to sleep with only half of their brain at a time, while the other half stays alert. They even keep one eye open, on the opposite side to the sleeping half of the brain.
Some birds use the same trick. Ducks sleeping in a row put the birds at each end on guard, with their outer eye open, watching for predators. Frigatebirds, which spend weeks flying over the ocean, can sleep in short bursts while gliding.
The amount of sleep also varies. Large plant-eaters such as elephants and giraffes sleep only a few hours a day, partly because they need so much time to find food and partly because lying down makes them vulnerable to predators. By contrast, the brown bat may sleep for around twenty hours a day.
Scientists are still not completely sure why sleep is necessary. One leading idea is that sleep allows the brain to clear away waste products that build up during the day. Another is that it helps to strengthen memories.

You will hear a talk about how vaccines work. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
To understand vaccines, we first need to understand the immune system. When a harmful microorganism, such as a virus or bacterium, enters the body, the immune system recognises molecules on its surface called antigens. It then produces antibodies, proteins that attach to the antigens and help destroy the invader.
The first time this happens, the response is slow, which is why we become ill. But the body keeps special cells called memory cells. If the same microorganism returns, these cells recognise it and produce antibodies so quickly that we often don't become ill at all. This is called immunity.
A vaccine allows the body to gain this immunity without having to suffer the disease. It contains antigens from a weakened or dead form of the microorganism, or, in some newer vaccines, instructions that tell our cells to make a harmless piece of it. The immune system responds as if it were a real infection and creates memory cells.
Some vaccines need booster doses, because the memory gradually fades.
Vaccines also protect people who can't be vaccinated themselves, such as newborn babies or people with weak immune systems. When enough people in a community are immune, the disease can't spread easily. This is called herd immunity. Thanks to vaccination, smallpox was completely eradicated, and polio has now disappeared from almost every country in the world.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Glass is one of the oldest materials made by humans, and one of the most surprising. It's made mainly from sand, or more precisely silica, heated to extremely high temperatures until it melts. Other substances, such as soda and lime, are added to lower the melting point and make the glass more durable.
Unlike most solids, glass has no regular crystal structure. Its atoms are arranged randomly, like a liquid, but they're frozen in place. This is why glass is transparent: light can pass through without being scattered.
You may have heard that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows over centuries. This is a myth. Old windows were made by spinning molten glass into a disc, which produced uneven sheets, and builders usually placed the thicker edge at the bottom for stability.
The earliest glass objects were beads, made in Mesopotamia about four thousand five hundred years ago. A major breakthrough came around two thousand years ago with glassblowing, which allowed people to make cheap containers quickly. Hyderabad in Sindh is still known for its traditional glass bangles.
Today, glass is used in ways the ancient glassmakers could never have imagined, most importantly in optical fibres. These thin strands carry internet data as pulses of light over huge distances under the sea.

You will hear a talk about the psychology of habits. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Psychologists estimate that a large part of what we do every day is driven by habit rather than conscious decisions. A habit, they say, has three parts. First there's a cue, a trigger that tells the brain to start the behaviour — for example, picking up your phone the moment you wake up. Then there's the routine, the behaviour itself. And finally there's the reward, the pleasant feeling that makes the brain want to repeat it.
Because habits are automatic, willpower alone is rarely enough to change them. A more effective strategy is to change your environment. If you want to eat fewer sweets, don't keep them in the house. If you want to read more, leave a book on your pillow.
Another useful technique is called 'habit stacking': attaching a new habit to an existing one. For instance, 'After I brush my teeth, I'll do five minutes of stretching.' The old habit acts as the cue for the new one.
How long does it take to form a habit? You may have heard the figure of twenty-one days, but research suggests the real time varies widely, from a few weeks to many months, depending on the person and the behaviour. Missing a single day doesn't ruin the process, so there's no need to give up after one mistake.

You will hear a talk about the role of fungi in nature. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
When people think of fungi, they usually picture mushrooms. But a mushroom is only the fruiting body of a much larger organism, like an apple on a tree. Most of the fungus lives hidden underground as a network of fine threads called hyphae, which together form a mycelium.
Fungi are neither plants nor animals. They can't make their own food from sunlight, as plants do. Instead, they feed by releasing chemicals called enzymes that break down material around them, then absorbing the nutrients.
This makes fungi essential decomposers. Without them, dead leaves and fallen trees would pile up in forests, and the nutrients locked inside them would never return to the soil.
Many fungi also form partnerships with plant roots, known as mycorrhizae. The fungus helps the plant absorb water and minerals, especially phosphorus, and in return the plant supplies the fungus with sugars. It's believed that around ninety per cent of land plants depend on these relationships.
Fungi have also changed human history. In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould called Penicillium killed bacteria, which led to the first widely used antibiotic. And of course, without yeast, another fungus, we would have no bread.

You will hear a talk about how cities can reduce flooding. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
As cities grow, more and more ground is covered in concrete and asphalt. These surfaces are impermeable, which means rainwater can't soak into the soil. Instead, it rushes into drains, which quickly overflow during heavy storms. Karachi and Lahore have both suffered serious urban flooding in recent monsoons.
Traditionally, engineers responded by building bigger drains and concrete channels to carry water away as fast as possible. But this often just moves the flooding further downstream.
A newer approach, sometimes called the 'sponge city' idea, was developed in China. Instead of getting rid of water quickly, cities are designed to absorb, store and slowly release it. Methods include permeable pavements, which let water through tiny gaps; rain gardens, which are shallow planted areas that collect water from roofs and roads; and green roofs covered in plants.
Parks can also be designed to flood safely. In some cities, sports fields are built slightly lower than the surrounding streets, so that during a storm they temporarily fill with water like a lake, protecting nearby homes.
Another benefit is that the stored water can recharge underground aquifers, which many cities rely on for drinking water. However, these methods require careful planning and regular maintenance — blocked gaps in a permeable pavement, for example, make it useless.

Mrs Haider: My other concern is fairness. Not every student has internet access at home.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)

Iqra: That must have made life much easier.
Grandfather: In some ways. But tractors are expensive, and many small farmers have fallen into debt paying for fuel and repairs.
Iqra: What about water? Did you have tube wells?
Grandfather: No, we depended on the canal and the rain. Tube wells came later. They were a blessing at first, but now the water table has dropped so much that wells have to be dug far deeper than before.
Iqra: I read that farmers now use a lot of chemical fertiliser.
Grandfather: Yes. At first the harvests doubled. But we used to put manure on the fields and rotate crops, growing beans or lentils to feed the soil. Now many farmers grow wheat and rice year after year, and the soil is getting tired.
Iqra: Is anything better now?
Grandfather: Of course! Mobile phones. Farmers can check market prices before selling, so middlemen can't cheat them so easily. And weather forecasts help us plan.
Iqra: So it's a mixture of good and bad.
Grandfather: That's farming — and life!
